article_content: In a candid conversation at the Brookings Institution, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton stood firmly behind President Obama’s decision to prolong nuclear negotiations with Iran — but with a clear condition: any agreement must fully and verifiably shut down every possible route to a nuclear weapon, including hidden ones. 'No deal is better than a bad deal,' she declared, emphasizing that trust must be earned through ironclad oversight. Clinton also took pride in having helped launch these talks during her time at the State Department, suggesting her fingerprints are on the current diplomatic process. She noted with approval that international partners haven’t walked away, even as talks stretch into another seven months. Reflecting on the 2009 Iranian protests, Clinton admitted she wishes she’d been louder in support of the demonstrators, recalling how the State Department once asked Twitter to delay maintenance so protesters could stay connected online. On Israel, she pushed back against criticism of the Obama White House, insisting the administration remains unwavering in its commitment to Israel’s safety — even amid heated rhetoric, like the leaked comment calling Prime Minister Netanyahu a derogatory name. 'We’re two loud democracies,' she said, shrugging off the friction as inevitable. And turning to domestic news, Clinton pointed to Friday’s strong jobs report as evidence the economy isn’t just bouncing back — it’s building momentum for the next two years.

article_content: In June 2023, India joined the Minerals Security Partnership (MSP)—a coalition of advanced economies formed in 2022 to build resilient, diversified supply chains for critical minerals essential to clean energy and national security. The move came amid close coordination with the United States ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s state visit. India’s inclusion was driven by three key factors: its massive consumer market, its pivotal role in achieving global climate goals, and its unique position as a leading voice of the Global South—countries often underrepresented in Western-led initiatives. The MSP seeks to counterbalance China’s overwhelming dominance in mining and processing minerals like lithium, cobalt, copper, and rare earth elements—materials indispensable for electric vehicle batteries, renewable energy systems, and advanced electronics. Demand for lithium alone is projected to surge more than 40-fold over the next decade due to the global shift toward electrified transportation. Australia leads global lithium production, followed by Chile and China. Yet, the MSP members aim to create end-to-end supply chains—from exploration to distribution—that are immune to disruptions caused by pandemics, geopolitical tensions, or monopolistic control. Geoffrey Pyatt, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Energy Resources, played a central role in brokering India’s entry. While he avoided calling it an ‘American demand,’ he acknowledged that both sides were aligned: 'We were both pushing on an open door.' He highlighted India’s ‘critical mass’—its economic scale, industrial ambition, and ability to bridge the Global North and South. 'India sits at the high table,' Pyatt noted, 'but also carries unique credibility with developing nations.' This dual identity made India indispensable to the MSP’s legitimacy and reach. India officially identified 30 critical minerals—including lithium, cobalt, graphite, and rare earth elements—in a June 2023 report by the Ministry of Mines. The report warned that geographic concentration of extraction and processing poses serious supply risks, implicitly targeting China, which controls over 70% of global lithium refining and nearly 80% of rare earth processing. Despite its ambitions, India remains a net importer of 10 of these 30 minerals. For example, it relies heavily on China for cobalt and on Chile, Russia, and Belgium for lithium. A revealing moment came when Pyatt visited Mahindra’s electric vehicle plant in Pune: despite enthusiasm for India’s electrification drive, engineers admitted their batteries came entirely from CATL, a Chinese firm. This dependency underscores the urgency behind India’s MSP membership—not just to diversify sources, but to build domestic capacity in mineral processing and battery manufacturing.

La demande de lithium seul devrait augmenter de plus de 40 fois au cours de la prochaine décennie en raison du passage mondial vers les transports électrifiés. L'Australie est le principal producteur mondial de lithium, suivie par le Chili et la Chine. Toutefois, les membres du MSP cherchent à créer des chaînes d'approvisionnement intégrées — de l'exploration à la distribution — capables de résister aux perturbations causées par des pandémies, des tensions géopolitiques ou un contrôle monopolistique. 'L'Inde siège à la table des grands,' a noté Pyatt, 'mais elle possède aussi une crédibilité unique auprès des nations en développement.' Cette identité double a rendu l'Inde indispensable à la légitimité et à la portée du MSP. L'Inde a officiellement identifié 30 minéraux critiques — y compris le lithium, le cobalt, le graphite et les terres rares — dans un rapport publié en juin 2023 par le ministère des Mines. Le rapport mettait en garde contre la concentration géographique de l'extraction et du traitement, visant implicitement la Chine, qui contrôle plus de 70 % du raffinage mondial du lithium et près de 80 % du traitement des terres rares. Malgré ses ambitions, l'Inde reste un importateur net de 10 de ces 30 minéraux. Par exemple, elle dépend fortement de la Chine pour le cobalt et du Chili, de la Russie et de la Belgique pour le lithium. Un moment révélateur est survenu lorsque Pyatt a visité l'usine de véhicules électriques de Mahindra à Pune : malgré l'enthousiasme pour la mobilité électrique en Inde, les ingénieurs ont admis que leurs batteries provenaient entièrement de CATL, une entreprise chinoise. Cette dépendance souligne l'urgence de l'adhésion de l'Inde au MSP — non seulement pour diversifier les sources, mais aussi pour développer une capacité domestique dans le traitement des minéraux et la fabrication de batteries.

article_content: Scientists have found evidence of at least 98 deaths and more graves than previously documented at the Dozier School for Boys in Marianna, Florida—a state-run reform school where students were allegedly brutally beaten, raped, and murdered. Researchers from the University of South Florida in Tampa identified at least 50 grave shafts on the campus, 19 more than the 31 recorded by the Florida Department of Law Enforcement during its 2010 investigation. In total, scientists estimate a minimum of 96 children—aged six to 18—and two adults died between 1911 and 1973, with many burials never officially recorded. Access to records after 1960 is restricted due to privacy laws, and dense vegetation has hindered full archaeological surveys, suggesting even more victims may remain undiscovered. The largest gravesite is on the northern edge of the campus, where African-American boys were buried. Thirty-one graves there are marked with white crosses, but researchers believe these markers do not align with actual burial locations. 'We anticipated finding about 25 to 30 grave shafts,' said Christian Wells, an assistant professor of anthropology who led the fieldwork. 'But we found a minimum of 50.' The school, opened in January 1900, was shut down in June 2011 after decades of abuse allegations. Former students, known as the 'White House Boys,' named for the building where much of the abuse occurred, have shared harrowing accounts of forced labor, torture, and fatal violence. Roger Dean Kiser, who was sent to Dozier at age 12 in 1959, wrote in his memoir, 'The White House Boys: An American Tragedy,' that the screams of other boys being beaten echoed through thick walls, and some were carried to the infirmary in wheelbarrows. Records indicate that more than 50 children were buried on-site, and over 30 were sent elsewhere—but 22 deaths went unrecorded. African-American boys were three times more likely to be buried in unmarked or undocumented graves than white boys. One case involved Thomas Curry, a white boy who died of blunt head trauma. Official records falsely claimed he died after escaping, but evidence suggests he was killed on campus. Owen Smith, sent to Dozier in 1940 after running away from home, vanished. His family was told he escaped, was recaptured, then returned to the school. A former student reported seeing him taken into the 'White House.' Weeks later, officials claimed his decomposing body was found under a house—yet neighbors said they heard nothing. Researchers plan to survey the southern part of the campus in January, where white boys were housed, expecting additional burial sites. 'I didn’t realize going in how much of a story of civil rights this was,' said Erin Kimmerle, another lead anthropologist.

Des chercheurs de l'Université de Floride du Sud à Tampa ont identifié au moins 50 puits funéraires sur le campus, 19 de plus que les 31 enregistrés par le Département de la loi de Floride lors de son enquête de 2010. Au total, les scientifiques estiment qu'au moins 96 enfants — âgés de six à 18 ans — et deux adultes sont morts entre 1911 et 1973, avec de nombreuses sépultures jamais officiellement enregistrées. L'accès aux dossiers après 1960 est restreint en raison de lois sur la vie privée, et la végétation dense a entravé les enquêtes archéologiques complètes, suggérant que davantage de victimes pourraient rester indéterminées. Le plus grand cimetière se trouve au nord du campus, où les garçons afro-américains étaient enterrés. Trente-et-une tombes sont marquées par des croix blanches, mais les chercheurs pensent que ces marqueurs ne correspondent pas aux véritables lieux d'inhumation. 'Nous prévisions de trouver environ 25 à 30 puits funéraires,' a déclaré Christian Wells, professeur adjoint en anthropologie qui a mené les travaux sur le terrain. 'Mais nous avons trouvé un minimum de 50.' L'école, ouverte en janvier 1900, a été fermée en juin 2011 après des décennies d'allégations d'abus. Anciens élèves, connus sous le nom de 'White House Boys', nommés ainsi en référence au bâtiment où la plupart des abus avaient lieu, ont partagé des récits horrifiants de travail forcé, de torture et de violence mortelle. Roger Dean Kiser, envoyé à Dozier à l'âge de 12 ans en 1959, a écrit dans son mémoire, 'Les Garçons de la Maison Blanche : Une tragédie américaine', que les cris des autres garçons battus résonnaient à travers les murs épais, et que certains étaient transportés à l'infirmerie dans des brouettes. Les dossiers indiquent que plus de 50 enfants ont été enterrés sur place, et plus de 30 ont été transférés ailleurs — mais 22 décès n'ont jamais été enregistrés. Les garçons afro-américains étaient trois fois plus susceptibles d'être enterrés dans des tombes non marquées ou non documentées que les garçons blancs. Un cas implique Thomas Curry, un garçon blanc qui est mort d'un traumatisme crânien. Les dossiers officiels affirmaient faussement qu'il était mort après une fuite, mais les preuves suggèrent qu'il a été tué sur le campus. Owen Smith, envoyé à Dozier en 1940 après avoir fugué de chez lui, a disparu. Sa famille a été informée qu'il s'était évadé, puis capturé, puis renvoyé à l'école. Un ancien élève a déclaré l'avoir vu emmené vers la 'Maison Blanche'. Des semaines plus tard, les autorités ont affirmé que son corps en décomposition avait été retrouvé sous une maison — alors que les voisins disent n'avoir rien entendu. Les chercheurs prévoient d'étudier la partie sud du campus en janvier, où vivaient les garçons blancs, en s'attendant à découvrir davantage de sépultures. 'Je ne réalisais pas en arrivant à quel point c'était une histoire de droits civiques,' a déclaré Erin Kimmerle, une autre anthropologue principale.

article_content: Gordon Brown’s closest aides prepared him for the role of Prime Minister by hurling insults such as 'Sod off, you Scottish git!' at him, it was revealed today. His former special adviser, Damian McBride, said he and other colleagues would shout abuse to 'get under the skin' of the former Labour leader, who would respond with his mantra: 'I will do my utmost.' Brown endured this verbal conditioning in his office as he prepared to succeed Tony Blair on June 27, 2007. McBride explained in a blog posted exactly five years after Brown entered Number 10 that the heckling was designed to simulate the hostility Brown would face from protesters outside Downing Street, where demonstrators had been calling Blair a 'war criminal.' 'It’s not often you’re paid to hurl abuse at someone about to become the most powerful person in the country,' McBride wrote. 'But given Iraq war protesters were already gathering at the gates to bid farewell to Tony Blair, we thought Brown should rehearse handling such distractions.' 'I often wondered what Treasury officials passing by must have thought, hearing Gordon boom, 'I will do my utmost,' while I screamed back: 'Sod off, you Scottish git!' 'Sue Nye’s heckles came straight out of Father Ted—'Booo!', 'Hiss!', 'You’re a very bad man!'—but I tried to escalate: 'Blood on your hands, Brown!' 'You’re a murderer!' 'Every so often, I’d say something that cut deep, and he’d stop mid-sentence and give me a long, chilling stare. I’d protest, 'Well, you can’t react like that if someone says it in the street!' — which only earned me another stare.' McBride’s blog offers a rare glimpse into the psychological preparation behind Brown’s premiership. However, he later resigned after sending malicious and false emails to fellow Labour strategist Derek Draper, targeting George Osborne and David Cameron with unfounded personal allegations. The blog also reveals Brown’s desire to scrap university tuition fees—a move he ultimately shelved out of fear of backlash from Blair’s allies. 'If he’d succeeded,' McBride noted, 'it would have strengthened his position to break from Blair-era policies early on.' Brown also struggled to bring key staff from the Treasury into Downing Street. 'He inherited brilliant civil servants,' McBride wrote, 'but without mutual trust or understanding, his natural tendency to micromanage resurfaced.'

Le billet de McBride offre un aperçu rare de la préparation psychologique derrière le mandat de Brown. Cependant, il a été contraint de démissionner après avoir envoyé des e-mails malveillants et faux à son collègue travailliste Derek Draper, diffamant George Osborne et David Cameron avec des allégations infondées sur leur vie privée. 'S’il avait réussi,' a noté McBride, 'cela aurait renforcé sa position pour rompre avec les politiques de l’ère Blair dès le début.' Brown a également eu du mal à recruter suffisamment de collaborateurs du Trésor à Downing Street. 'Il a hérité de fonctionnaires brillants et compétents,' a écrit McBride, 'mais, faute de confiance mutuelle et de compréhension commune, son penchant naturel au micromanagement est réapparu.'

article_content: A Saudi activist, Raif Badawi, who was sentenced to 1,000 lashes and 10 years in prison for founding an online forum that encouraged open dialogue about faith, will not undergo his second round of flogging this Friday. His wife, Ensaf Haida, confirmed the delay, attributing it to medical advice following his first flogging on January 9. According to Amnesty International, a physician determined that Badawi’s wounds had not healed sufficiently to endure further punishment. While the postponement has been welcomed by his supporters—including friend Ali Rizvi, who called it 'definitely encouraging'—they stress that the underlying injustice remains unresolved. The Saudi government has yet to officially comment, but international pressure continues to mount, with the U.S. State Department and global rights groups demanding the immediate cancellation of all corporal punishment. Critics argue that even the temporary halt highlights the extreme cruelty of the sentence itself, originally handed down in 2014 for actions dating back to 2008.

Sa femme, Ensaf Haida, a confirmé le report, l'attribuant à un avis médical suite à sa première flagellation le 9 janvier. Selon Amnesty International, un médecin a estimé que les blessures de Badawi n'étaient pas encore suffisamment cicatrisées pour supporter davantage de châtiments. Bien que ce report soit accueilli avec soulagement par ses partisans — dont l'ami Ali Rizvi, qui l'a qualifié de 'certainement encourageant' — ils soulignent que l'injustice fondamentale persiste. Le gouvernement saoudien n'a pas encore officiellement commenté, mais la pression internationale s'intensifie, avec le Département d'État américain et des organisations de défense des droits humains exigeant l'annulation immédiate de toutes les peines corporelles. Les critiques affirment que même cet arrêt temporaire révèle l'extrême cruauté de la peine elle-même, prononcée en 2014 pour des actes datant de 2008.

article_content: Peter Trythall, headmaster of Stanbridge Earls School in rural Hampshire, has resigned amid shocking allegations of sexual abuse and institutional failure. His departure, described as being 'in the best interests of the school,' comes as a major police investigation continues into claims made by two former students — including a vulnerable young girl who suffered appalling abuse. The £39,000-per-year school, which supports children with learning disabilities, was previously found by a tribunal to have discriminated against the girl and failed to act on her repeated complaints of pain in an intimate area. Staff were criticized for being 'unsystematic, unprofessional, ad hoc and completely inadequate' in their duty to protect her. Trythall was specifically accused of 'a failure of responsibility.' The Nursing and Midwifery Council has confirmed that school nurse Melanie Bavington is under investigation. Meanwhile, two governors — Tony Knight and Claire Marsden — have also resigned. The Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal ordered the school to pay £86,000 in legal costs to the victim’s family. The girl cannot be named for legal reasons. Detectives from Hampshire Constabulary’s Public Protection Department are now examining whether further criminal offenses were committed against other students at the school. In response, the school’s governing body has pledged urgent reforms and plans to collaborate with external agencies. Day-to-day operations are now overseen by two deputy heads, supported by a specialist SEN leadership consultant and the Chairman of Governors, pending the appointment of an interim head.

article_content: Serena Williams bounced back from her disappointing loss to Simona Halep with a commanding 6-1, 6-1 victory over Eugenie Bouchard at the WTA Finals in Singapore. The world No. 1 suffered her worst defeat in 16 years in her previous match, winning just two games — her first loss in 17 matches at the WTA Finals. That result left her reliant on other outcomes to secure a semifinal berth. Williams delivered a dominant performance, sealing the win in just 57 minutes. Her victory also ensured Simona Halep became the first player to qualify for the semifinals, as Halep needed Bouchard to win only one game. Though Bouchard fought off a 0-40 deficit to hold serve in the first set, she struggled overall, having entered the tournament hampered by a thigh injury and losing all her round-robin matches in straight sets. Despite the win, Williams still needs help to advance. In the Red Group, Halep faces Ana Ivanovic on Friday; if Ivanovic wins in straight sets, she will advance and eliminate Williams. In the White Group, Caroline Wozniacki secured her second consecutive win by defeating Agnieszka Radwanska 7-5, 6-3. The match featured intense rallies and sharp shot-making, and Wozniacki, the lowest-ranked player in the field, admitted to being awestruck by her opponent’s play: 'I kept thinking, 'Aga, how did you make that ball?' However, Wozniacki’s semifinal fate remains uncertain. Petra Kvitova defeated Maria Sharapova 6-3, 6-2 in the other White Group match — her first win over Sharapova in six attempts since 2011. With all four players still in contention, every result matters heading into the final round-robin matches.

article_content: An Air France Airbus A340 operated for five days with 30 critical screws missing from a protective panel on its wing — a lapse only detected after the plane landed in Boston. The aircraft had recently undergone routine maintenance in Xiamen, China, before flights to Paris and then the United States. Once identified, technicians replaced the loose panel, grounding the plane until repairs were completed. Details emerged from an internal union document leaked to AFP. While Air France insists that flight safety was never at risk — noting the panel was non-structural — aviation experts caution that detached components in flight can strike vital systems. The airline attributes the error to its contracted maintenance team in Xiamen, where cost-saving measures make it a popular service hub. Union representatives called the oversight 'deplorable,' pointing out it wasn't the first such mistake: last year, a Boeing 747 was grounded after being repainted with flammable coating during a similar China-based service. The article also recalls three major past Air France tragedies — the 2000 Concorde crash, the 2005 Toronto runway overrun, and the 2009 Atlantic disappearance — though none were caused by missing screws, their mention reflects broader public concern over maintenance reliability.

article_content: Two of the sharpest dressers in football—Sky Sports’ new mega-signing, Thierry Henry, and veteran pundit Graeme Souness—were paired for the Frenchman’s much-anticipated Super Sunday debut. Nothing off the peg there. After a fortnight of Henry’s arrival being heralded with generous on-screen coverage—and presenter Ed Chamberlin looking none too shabby either—they got down to business. An early and legitimate test of whether a great player turned pundit will deliver on air is when asked to reflect on the fortunes of his former club. Henry’s new teammates, Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher, both passed that test with flying colors. Thierry Henry fared extremely well on his Sky Sports debut on Sunday afternoon. Alongside the experienced Graeme Souness, he looked dapper as he spoke about his old club, Arsenal. When Chamberlin posed a lunchtime question on whether Arsenal had regressed over the past 12 months, it was significant that Henry didn’t dodge it. 'Yes,' he said. 'It looks like a team aiming to finish fourth—which isn't Arsenal. You want to win the title. They need to defend better—not just the back four. It has to be a team effort. They bought Mertesacker, but does he have protection? They're not far off, but they're missing a big piece—a Vieira and a Gilberto Silva.' To illustrate how settled he is as a pundit, Souness quipped: 'Would you like your daughter to date any of the Arsenal players? They're a team of son-in-laws—all nice guys. You need a few rascals.' Henry believes Arsenal lack a midfield protector like former captain Patrick Vieira. He also spoke highly of former teammate Gilberto Silva during his Sky Sports debut. Previewing West Ham versus Hull City, Henry singled out West Ham’s former Arsenal player Alex Song as someone who 'would improve Arsenal.' Henry is understated, but his studio work for the BBC during last summer’s World Cup showed he can deliver intelligent, incisive analysis. With a goalless first half at Upton Park, Henry offered his perspective on frontline play. When Hull’s Sone Aluko stayed on his feet after being challenged from behind by James Tomkins in the penalty area, Henry remarked: 'If you touch me, I go down in the box. If you stick your leg out like that from behind after you’ve been beaten, you’re asking for trouble. That should’ve been a penalty—if he’d gone down, which he didn’t.' In the build-up to Manchester City’s match, Henry praised City’s David Silva and noted that Alexis Sánchez’s form at Arsenal stems from receiving consistent touches—unlike at Barcelona. As Arsenal took a 1-0 lead through Santi Cazorla’s penalty, Henry explained how the visitors had neutralized Silva: 'There’s always a man between the ball and David Silva.' His verdict on the penalty? 'It was for me.' And, to be fair, so was Souness’s. Arsenal completed a masterful 2-0 win, and Henry focused on the team’s unexpectedly different approach: 'Usually, Arsenal win games by passing and being brilliant with the ball. Not today. They defended well as a unit… 34% possession was enough to win.' It was, Henry suggested, a match where Arsenal showed 'commitment, desire, and togetherness.' Qualities Sky Sports hope they’ll get in abundance from their new star signing. On this showing, he looks tailor-made for the role.

article_content: Customers who are owed a total of £153 million by major UK energy suppliers may soon receive their money back, under a new industry-wide scheme unveiled today. Over the past six years, billions of pounds in overpayments — made by customers who switched to cheaper providers while still holding credit balances — were retained by energy firms instead of being refunded. These funds, often left behind when customers moved homes or failed to provide final meter readings, became an unintended windfall for suppliers. Following pressure from Ofgem, the UK’s energy regulator, the six largest energy companies have agreed to a plan to return unclaimed credits to customers or redirect them toward broader consumer benefits. Ofgem’s CEO, Dermot Nolan, welcomed the move as a necessary first step toward rebuilding public trust, emphasizing that repayment is the bare minimum expected of energy firms. He warned that failure to fully implement the plan could lead to regulatory enforcement. To assist customers, Energy UK — the industry trade body — has launched the website myenergycredit.com, where individuals can check if they’re owed money. Former customers are urged to contact their previous suppliers, even if they believe they didn’t leave a forwarding address or final meter reading. For credits that remain unclaimed after two years, suppliers will now allocate the funds to support vulnerable households. A total of £38 million will be donated over the first two years, with projections estimating £65 million annually by 2018. Suppliers will clearly communicate this policy moving forward. Amber Rudd, Minister of Energy and Climate Change, affirmed that returning customers’ money is a matter of fairness. Meanwhile, Energy UK’s CEO Angela Knight described the initiative as a 'great campaign' and encouraged former customers to claim what’s theirs. The article also includes consumer advice: regularly comparing energy tariffs — ideally every six to twelve months — can save households up to £300 per year. Online tariffs typically offer the lowest rates, and prices vary regionally, so shoppers should compare based on their location.

article_content: According to a recent Gallup poll, Mitt Romney holds a seven-point lead among early voters, with 52% supporting him compared to President Barack Obama’s 45%. This group represents about 15% of total voters who have already cast their ballots. As Hurricane Sandy devastated the East Coast, both candidates suspended campaign events to focus on disaster response. Obama cut short trips to Florida and Wisconsin, returned to Washington, and held briefings with emergency officials. He warned the public that recovery would be slow and acknowledged the storm’s potential economic toll, particularly on New York’s financial sector. Romney similarly paused all public appearances with running mate Paul Ryan. He maintained a measured tone, calling FEMA Deputy Administrator Richard Serino to express support and cautioning that damage would be severe — aligning his messaging with Obama’s without overt criticism. First Lady Michelle Obama underscored her husband’s commitment to public safety, stating he was prioritizing the well-being of Americans above politics. Meanwhile, Virginia Governor Bob McDonnell announced extended early voting hours and rapid restoration of power to polling sites, while Maryland temporarily closed its early voting centers. Gallup’s overall likely voter numbers remain tied at 49% each, suggesting early voters may determine the election’s outcome. With projected damages between $10 billion and $20 billion, Sandy ranks among the costliest natural disasters in U.S. history. Obama’s team drew lessons from President George W. Bush’s poorly received response to Hurricane Katrina, ensuring visible, proactive leadership. Romney’s advisers, including Kevin Madden, deliberately avoided politicizing the storm, emphasizing: 'We try to focus on the things that we can control.' Despite the disruption, campaign ads and messaging from both sides continued. Yet Obama’s televised appearances and authoritative tone dominated media coverage, reinforcing perceptions of leadership — even as he carried the risk of being held accountable for any federal response failures.

article_content: In the quiet coastal village of Port Isaac, famous for being the filming location of the beloved TV series Doc Martin, a shocking revelation has shaken the community. Paul Williams, the owner of The Bay Hotel—a building that doubles as 'Wenn House' on screen—was exposed as a convicted fraudster whose past crimes targeted vulnerable elderly people. The truth came to light through a covert campaign: anonymous emails, hand-printed posters nailed to lampposts, and USB drives left on doorsteps. These materials revealed that in 2006, Williams was sentenced to 18 months in prison after a judge branded him a 'charlatan' who preyed on the grief of widows and the trust of the blind. One victim was led to believe her deceased husband had guided her to a forged will hidden inside a grandfather clock; another, an 82-year-old man with vision loss, lost money to a fake psychic scheme. After serving his sentence, Williams relocated to Port Isaac, reinventing himself as a charming local figure. He cultivated friendships with the Doc Martin cast, regaling guests with tales of his supposed days as the drummer for 1980s band Dexy’s Midnight Runners—claims later proven false. His hotel thrived, becoming a hub for fans and celebrities alike. But not everyone believed his story. Tom Lane, owner of The Edge restaurant across the street, grew suspicious after investing £5,000 in the business in 2011. Lane complained Williams never worked as promised, spending instead long afternoons sipping tea and spinning tall tales. When Lane bought out Williams’s share for £40,000, the partnership dissolved—and so did the peace. When the exposé began circulating, suspicion turned to Lane. Police investigated, seizing his computer—but eventually returned it with no charges filed. Williams, confronted with the evidence, admitted to his past misdeeds but insisted the campaign was personal vengeance. He claimed the harassment escalated to threats and even tampering with his car’s brakes. 'I made mistakes,' he said. 'I paid for them. I quit drinking, stopped using drugs, and rebuilt my life. I turned this hotel from a wreck into something people love.' Yet the fallout continues. With Doc Martin rumored to end after its upcoming season, tourism may collapse. Williams now stays mostly indoors. His wife, Katie—a flutist—and their toddler daughter haven’t been seen in the village since last year. The dream of a fresh start in paradise has unraveled, leaving behind questions about redemption, revenge, and what happens when fiction and reality blur in a place built on storytelling.

article_content: In a stunning display of resilience, Chelsea overturned a halftime deficit to defeat Basel 3-1 at Stamford Bridge, sealing a 5-3 aggregate win and booking their place in the Europa League final. After Mohamed Salah’s last-gasp strike in the first half gave Basel hope, Chelsea exploded in the second half with three goals in just ten minutes. Fernando Torres opened the floodgates after capitalizing on a defensive rebound from Frank Lampard’s saved shot. Minutes later, Victor Moses pounced on a deflection off Torres’ low drive to make it 3-2. Brazilian defender David Luiz then stunned the crowd with a curling masterpiece from outside the box, effectively ending Basel’s resistance. Despite Fabian Frei rattling the crossbar, the Swiss side couldn’t recover. Meanwhile, Benfica fought back from a 1-0 first-leg deficit to beat Fenerbahçe 3-1 at home, with Oscar Cardozo netting twice—once before and once after halftime—to clinch a 3-2 aggregate triumph. The stage is now set for a final showdown in Amsterdam on May 15, where Benitez, often criticized by Chelsea fans, will aim to secure his only tangible success during his turbulent tenure. Though supporters initially chanted for Jose Mourinho, the final whistle brought relief and pride. For Benfica, it’s their first European final since 1990—a historic return after decades of near misses.

article_content: On a clear day in June 2009, a mid-air collision occurred near Abingdon, Oxfordshire, between an RAF Grob Tutor 115E training aircraft and a civilian glider. The crash claimed the lives of 15-year-old air cadet Nicholas Rice and RAF reservist Flight Lieutenant Mike Blee, 62. Glider pilot Albert Freeborn, 29, survived the collision by parachuting to safety. At an inquest held at Oxford Coroner’s Court on 14 February 2012, Freeborn recounted how he heard the distinct sound of a nearby aircraft engine — a warning sign he recognized immediately. 'It’s very audible, and alarming,' he said. 'You know it has to be very close.' Moments later, he looked left and down and saw the Tutor directly beneath him. To his disbelief, the plane suddenly rotated upward and collided with his glider. The impact shattered the glider’s canopy and sent it into a violent nose-down spin. With the aircraft now inverted, Freeborn used his left hand to open the canopy and, supported by his harness, released the straps with his right hand. Gravity helped him clear the wreckage, and he pulled the parachute cord just as the glider spiraled toward the ground. As he descended, Freeborn observed the glider falling like a sycamore leaf, followed by the Tutor — its engine still running, trailing smoke — before it struck a crop field. Freeborn landed unharmed in a nearby field, just half a mile from the wreckage. Though physically uninjured, Freeborn revealed he has struggled with post-traumatic stress since the tragedy. The investigation confirmed flying conditions were excellent at the time of the accident.

'C'est très audible et alarmant', a-t-il dit. 'Vous savez qu'il doit être très proche.' Quelques instants plus tard, il a regardé vers la gauche et vers le bas et a vu le Tutor directement sous lui. À son grand étonnement, l'avion a soudainement pivoté vers le haut et a heurté son planeur. L'impact a brisé le cockpit du planeur et l'a envoyé en vrille violente la tête la première. L'appareil étant maintenant à l'envers, Freeborn a utilisé sa main gauche pour ouvrir le hublot et, soutenu par ses harnais, a libéré les sangles avec sa main droite. La gravité l'a aidé à s'éloigner de l'épave, et il a tiré sur l'anneau de parachute juste au moment où le planeur plongeait vers le sol. Pendant sa descente, Freeborn a observé le planeur tomber comme une feuille de sycomore, suivi par le Tutor — son moteur toujours en marche, laissant une traînée de fumée — avant qu'il ne percute un champ de culture. Freeborn s'est posé sans blessure dans un champ voisin, à seulement huit cents mètres des débris. Bien que physiquement indemne, Freeborn a révélé qu'il souffre depuis lors de troubles de stress post-traumatique. L'enquête a confirmé que les conditions de vol étaient excellentes au moment de l'accident.

RSPCA inspectors describe the blows as delivered 'with considerable force,' noting visible signs of fear in the dog. The charity has released the video in an effort to identify the individual responsible. The dog, whose breed remains unidentified, is thought to be a bull-type with distinctive white markings on the chest and front legs. RSPCA Inspector Laura Sayer stated, 'You can clearly see the dog being punched in the head with considerable force, several times. We are deeply concerned for its welfare.' Anyone with information is urged to contact the RSPCA at 0300 123 8018.

article_content: When the UK government hired Goldman Sachs to help sell Royal Mail shares, critics didn’t hold back — comparing the move to hiring Ronnie Biggs to guard a cash vault. Lawmakers on the Business, Innovation and Skills Committee were stunned to learn that ministers had no knowledge of Goldman Sachs’ recent $7.5 million settlement related to its role in the 1999 IPO of eToys Inc., an online toy retailer whose shares later quadrupled before the company collapsed. Business Secretary Vince Cable acknowledged full responsibility for setting Royal Mail’s initial share price at £3.30 — a figure that has since climbed past £5.60, turning the privatization into a financial windfall for early investors. The company’s first earnings report showed operating profits nearly doubling to £283 million, though part of that gain came from a £95 million VAT rebate and lower-than-expected restructuring costs. While parcel delivery growth stalled during the summer heatwave and strike threats hurt holiday-season business, Royal Mail noted that new size-based pricing and rising energy bills (which spurred more mail advertising) helped offset losses. Still, MPs questioned how such a prominent red flag — publicly documented on Google — could have been overlooked when selecting financial advisers. Mark Russell, head of the Shareholder Executive, admitted the team simply wasn’t aware of the eToys case. Committee chair Adrian Bailey called it ‘astonishing’ that such a well-known legal issue hadn’t factored into their decision-making. Cable stood by his position, insisting the sale was professionally handled, fair to taxpayers, and crucial for securing Royal Mail’s future as a six-day-a-week postal service — even if early gains felt like ‘froth’ to him.

Les députés de la commission des affaires, de l'innovation et des compétences étaient stupéfaits d'apprendre que les ministres ignoraient totalement le règlement récent de 7,5 millions de dollars de Goldman Sachs lié à son rôle lors de l'OPI de eToys Inc. en 1999, une entreprise de jouets en ligne dont les actions avaient quadruplé avant que l'entreprise ne fasse faillite. article_content: After parting ways with Everton, Samuel Eto'o has officially joined Sampdoria on a free transfer, as confirmed over the weekend. The 33-year-old striker, already a legend of the game, arrived in Rome for his medical ahead of a scheduled unveiling ahead of Sampdoria’s home clash with Palermo. Coach Sinisa Mihajlovic, aware of the buzz surrounding the signing, urged his squad to stay grounded. 'What party?' he asked at a press conference. 'Eto'o is a phenomenal player — four league titles, three Champions Leagues, record scorer for Cameroon — but this team got to third place because of hard work, not headlines. We don’t need distractions, we need focus.' Eto'o, who moved to Everton from Chelsea last August, retired from international duty shortly after, ending a storied career with 118 caps and 56 goals for Cameroon. Sampdoria, sitting joint-third in Serie A with Napoli on 33 points from 19 games, hope his presence adds both firepower and leadership — without tipping the team’s balance.

L'entraîneur Sinisa Mihajlovic, conscient de l'agitation entourant ce transfert, a exhorté ses joueurs à rester concentrés. 'Quelle fête ?' a-t-il demandé lors d'une conférence de presse. 'Eto'o est un joueur phénoménal — quatre titres de champion, trois Ligue des champions, meilleur buteur historique du Cameroun — mais cette équipe est arrivée à la troisième place grâce au travail acharné, pas aux articles médiatiques. Nous n'avons pas besoin de distractions, nous avons besoin de concentration.' Eto'o, qui avait rejoint Everton depuis Chelsea en août dernier, a pris sa retraite internationale peu après, mettant fin à une carrière mémorable avec 118 sélections et 56 buts pour le Cameroun. Sampdoria, à égalité avec Naples en troisième position du classement de Serie A avec 33 points en 19 matchs, espère que sa présence apportera à la fois puissance offensive et leadership, sans déséquilibrer l'équipe.

article_content: In Ankeny, Iowa, a 13-year-old girl and a 14-year-old boy were allegedly confined to the basement of their adoptive home for nearly a month, according to authorities. Their parents, Paul and JoAnn Drake, were charged with child abuse and false imprisonment after police discovered the children were only allowed out to attend school. Meals were slid under the locked basement door, and the children were required to return immediately after school. The Drakes told investigators the confinement was intended as discipline for behavioral issues. The situation was reported in September when one of the children spoke to a school employee, triggering involvement from the Department of Human Services. The teens were removed from the home on October 5. Three other children living in the household were not subjected to similar treatment. Married since 1989, the Drakes publicly identify as devout Christians, according to their Facebook profiles — though they have not responded to media requests. Released on bail from Polk County Jail, they now face up to 10 years in prison if convicted; a trial date has not yet been set.

article_content: Today, 96-year-old RAF bomber navigator Jim Stafford and his wife Betty, 95, are celebrating 70 years of marriage — a milestone made all the more remarkable by the fact that Jim survived five plane crashes during and after World War II. Jim, who joined the Royal Air Force in 1940, endured four crashes during wartime missions across the Middle East and South Africa, and a fifth shortly after the war ended in 1946. None resulted in serious injury. Mechanical failures — including hydraulic malfunctions and landing gear malfunctions — caused the crashes. One occurred when the aircraft ran out of fuel during a training flight over the Lake District. The couple first met in 1942 at Welling Gospel Chapel. 'That was when we saw each other for the first time properly,' Betty recalls. 'I guess we both quite liked what we saw.' Jim secured two weeks’ leave from the front lines to marry Betty in 1943. After the war, they settled in Felixstowe, where Jim became a schoolteacher and later a Methodist preacher — serving until he was 90. Betty worked for Favor Parker and the Felixstowe Dock and Railway Company, often accompanying Jim’s preaching tours as a piano soloist. Together, they raised two children — Malcolm and Veronica — and now enjoy six grandchildren and one great-grandchild. 'Love got us through,' says Betty. Jim adds: 'Not many people can say they’ve done that in their lives.'

Jim, qui a rejoint la Royal Air Force en 1940, a subi quatre crashs lors de missions de guerre au Moyen-Orient et en Afrique du Sud, ainsi qu'un cinquième peu après la fin de la guerre en 1946. Aucun n'a entraîné de blessures graves. Des pannes mécaniques — notamment des défaillances hydrauliques et des problèmes d'atterrissage des trains d'atterrissage — ont causé ces accidents. L'un d'eux s'est produit lorsque l'avion a manqué de carburant pendant un exercice d'entraînement dans le Lake District. Le couple s'est rencontré pour la première fois en 1942 à la chapelle évangélique de Welling. 'C'était la première fois que nous nous voyions vraiment,' se souvient Betty. 'Je pense que nous avons tous les deux aimé ce que nous avons vu.' Jim a obtenu deux semaines de congé du front pour épouser Betty en 1943. Après la guerre, ils se sont installés à Felixstowe, où Jim est devenu professeur, puis prédicateur méthodiste — il a continué jusqu'à l'âge de 90 ans. Betty a travaillé pour Favor Parker et la Felixstowe Dock and Railway Company, accompagnant souvent les tournées de prédication de Jim en tant que pianiste soliste. Ensemble, ils ont élevé deux enfants — Malcolm et Veronica — et comptent aujourd'hui six petits-enfants et un arrière-petit-enfant. 'L'amour nous a fait traverser cela,' dit Betty. Jim ajoute : 'Peu de gens peuvent dire qu'ils ont vécu ça.'

article_content: Wall Street markets suffered sharp declines as fears grew that Europe’s plan to save the euro might unravel before it could even take effect. Greek Prime Minister George Papandreou announced he would put the country’s bailout agreement to a public referendum, throwing the long-awaited deal into disarray. Financial markets around the world reacted violently. U.S. stocks fell by as much as 3%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 295 points, or 2.5%, at 11,660; the S&P 500 dropped 35 points, or 2.8%, to 1,218; and the Nasdaq fell 77 points, or 2.9%, to 2,607. German Chancellor Angela Merkel and French President Nicolas Sarkozy convened an emergency meeting, agreeing that Greece’s move made it more urgent than ever to advance the EU summit agreement. They planned to meet with Greek officials, the IMF, and other European partners in Cannes ahead of the G20 summit. In a surprising move, the Greek government dismissed all its defense chiefs without clear explanation, further unsettling investors and citizens alike. Investment strategist Paul Mendelsohn said, 'The market did not see this Greek referendum coming — which is potentially a killer. It could knock the wheels off the bus of the entire European rescue plan.' Britain’s FTSE fell 2%, while Germany’s DAX and France’s CAC-40 both plunged 5%. Across Asia, stock markets dropped as factory activity in key export economies slowed to near three-year lows in October. China’s manufacturing activity hit its lowest level since February 2009, reflecting a sharp decline in new export orders. The U.S. dollar index rose 1.5%, while oil futures dropped 2.7% and copper prices fell 3.8%. Japan’s Nikkei closed down 1.7%, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng lost 2.5%. The turmoil also prompted U.S. brokerage MF Global to file for bankruptcy after heavy losses on eurozone bonds. Founded in 1974, MF Global was led at the time by former New Jersey governor and Goldman Sachs CEO Jon Corzine. Papandreou’s announcement that voters would decide on a €100 billion bailout — including a 50% debt write-off and years of harsh austerity — marked Greece’s first referendum since 1974. A 'no' vote could trigger a disorderly default and potential exit from the eurozone. Recent polls showed 59% of Greeks viewed the package negatively, while 60% opposed the austerity measures. Yet, broader support remained for staying in the eurozone. Investors doubted Papandreou could win the vote. Greece’s main opposition party called for his resignation, accusing him of incompetence and political blackmail. Papandreou defended the referendum as a 'supreme act of democracy,' aiming to restore public trust. The Papandreou family has dominated Greek politics for decades: George Sr. served three terms (1944–45, 1963, 1964–65); Andreas Papandreou served two (1981–89, 1993–96); and George Jr. became prime minister in 2009. Despite past popularity, his leadership is now deeply tarnished by the financial crisis. Elected in a landslide in 2009 on promises of economic revival, Papandreou was forced into austerity after revelations that Greece’s deficit was far worse than reported. National strikes followed. Public trust collapsed: by May 2011, 77% expressed no confidence in his handling of the crisis. He barely survived a no-confidence vote the following month.

La chancelière allemande Angela Merkel et le président français Nicolas Sarkozy ont convoqué une réunion d'urgence, convenant que la décision grecque rendait plus urgente que jamais l'avancée de l'accord du sommet de l'UE. Ils prévoyaient de rencontrer les responsables grecs, le FMI et d'autres partenaires européens à Cannes, avant le sommet du G20. Dans un mouvement surprenant, le gouvernement grec a limogé tous ses chefs de la défense sans explication claire, ajoutant à l'inquiétude des investisseurs et des citoyens. L'analyste en investissement Paul Mendelsohn a déclaré : 'Le marché n'a pas vu venir ce référendum grec — ce qui est potentiellement un coup fatal. Il pourrait faire tomber toute la stratégie de sauvetage européen.' L'indice britannique FTSE a chuté de 2 %, tandis que le DAX allemand et le CAC-40 français ont plongé de 5 %. Dans toute l'Asie, les marchés boursiers ont baissé alors que l'activité manufacturière dans les grandes puissances d'exportation a ralenti à des niveaux proches de leurs plus bas depuis trois ans en octobre. L'activité manufacturière en Chine a atteint son plus bas niveau depuis février 2009, reflétant un net recul des commandes d'exportation. L'indice du dollar américain a augmenté de 1,5 %, tandis que les cours du pétrole ont baissé de 2,7 % et ceux du cuivre de 3,8 %. Le Nikkei japonais a clôturé en baisse de 1,7 %, et le Hang Seng de Hong Kong a perdu 2,5 %. Cette turbulence a également poussé la société de courtage américaine MF Global à déposer son bilan après des pertes massives sur les obligations de la zone euro. Fondée en 1974, MF Global était dirigée à cette époque par l'ancien gouverneur du New Jersey et ancien PDG de Goldman Sachs, Jon Corzine. L'annonce de Papandreou selon laquelle les électeurs décideraient d'un plan de sauvetage de 100 milliards d'euros — incluant une réduction de 50 % de la dette et des années d'austérité sévère — marque le premier référendum grec depuis 1974. Un vote 'non' pourrait déclencher une faillite désordonnée et une sortie potentielle de la zone euro. Des sondages récents montrent que 59 % des Grecs considèrent le paquet comme négatif, tandis que 60 % s'opposent aux mesures d'austérité. Pourtant, un soutien plus large demeure pour rester dans l'euro. Les investisseurs doutent que Papandreou puisse remporter le vote. Le principal parti d'opposition grec a exigé sa démission, l'accusant d'incompétence et de chantage politique. Papandreou a défendu le référendum comme un 'acte suprême de démocratie', visant à restaurer la confiance publique. La famille Papandreou a dominé la politique grecque pendant des décennies : George Sr. a occupé trois mandats (1944–45, 1963, 1964–65) ; Andreas Papandreou deux (1981–89, 1993–96) ; et George Jr. est devenu premier ministre en 2009. Malgré sa popularité passée, son leadership est désormais profondément entaché par la crise financière. Élu à une large majorité en 2009 avec des promesses de redressement économique, Papandreou a été contraint d'adopter des mesures d'austérité après la révélation que le déficit grec était bien plus élevé que prévu. Des grèves nationales ont suivi. La confiance du public s'est effondrée : en mai 2011, 77 % exprimaient leur manque de confiance dans sa gestion de la crise. Il a à peine survécu à un vote de défiance le mois suivant.

article_content: 'We must play on' was Michael Clarke’s message to his teammates when he spoke movingly at Phillip Hughes’ funeral. And play on he did — declaring himself emotionally ready to lead Australia in the first Test since Hughes’ death. While Clarke’s hamstring had been a physical concern leading up to the rearranged match, the deeper wound was his broken heart — emotions that would take far longer to heal. At the funeral, Clarke spoke of feeling Hughes’ spirit around him. That presence will be palpable at the Adelaide Oval on Tuesday, where the team honored Hughes by naming him as their 13th man. A state memorial service originally scheduled for the Sydney Cricket Ground has been canceled, following consultation between Cricket Australia and the Hughes family. New South Wales Premier Mike Baird explained the decision: 'All parties felt that, given the enormous outpouring of support at last Wednesday’s funeral, a state memorial service would no longer be necessary.' Captain Michael Clarke inspected the pitch during an Australian net session at the Adelaide Oval on Monday. The number 408 — Hughes’ Test cap number — was prominently displayed on the ground and on players’ shirts, along with black armbands. In tribute to their fallen teammate, Australia’s playing XI included Clarke (captain), Brad Haddin (wicketkeeper), Ryan Harris, Mitchell Johnson, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Marsh, Chris Rogers, Peter Siddle, Steve Smith, David Warner, and Shane Watson. Josh Hazlewood and Shaun Marsh were left out. Clarke was excused from the traditional pre-Test media conference. Mitchell Johnson announced the team, praising Clarke’s strength: 'It’s a huge boost to have him back playing for us. His captaincy — and how strong he’s been through this tragedy — means everything. We just want him to score runs and be that aggressive leader.' Johnson, Australia’s chief fast bowler, was asked about his use of the bouncer — a delivery that had previously left Kevin Pietersen feeling 'petrified' during the Ashes. 'We’ve got to play the way we’ve been playing — aggressively. If that means bowling short, we’ll do it. We’re not changing a thing.' Virat Kohli, captaining India for the first time in place of the injured MS Dhoni, echoed this sentiment: 'I don’t think that’s even up for debate. The bouncer is part of cricket — it’s every bowler’s right to use it. If it fits our plan, we’ll use it. We won’t drift from our game.' Kohli, who was close to Hughes, recalled meeting him during a 2008 camp in Brisbane and said, 'After attending the funeral, I was deeply moved. Phil was someone I interacted with regularly on tour. It was equally heartbreaking for me.' But he added, 'As professional cricketers, we have to move on — and play the Test match.' On Tuesday, the Adelaide crowd will observe 63 seconds of applause before play begins — honoring Hughes’ score of 63 not out when he was struck at the SCG on November 25. Players will wear his Test cap number, 408, on their shirts.

article_content: Editor's note: Bishop T.D. Jakes is the founder and senior pastor of The Potter’s House in Dallas, Texas — a multiracial, nondenominational church with more than 50 outreach ministries. In a heartfelt reflection, he writes: 'It is a victory for democracy that proves our country provides possibilities for all people.' Last night, like most Americans, I watched with goosebumps as history unfolded. Sitting beside my 13-year-old son, I gazed from the television screen to his eyes as Senator Barack Obama became the first African American to secure a major-party presidential nomination — the Democratic Party’s ticket for the presidency. I congratulate Senator Obama on this extraordinary milestone. Thank you for accepting the torch passed down by our forefathers — carrying it through decades of struggle, trial, and injustice — and lighting the way for a new generation. You faced those who said 'No,' 'You can’t win,' or 'It will never happen,' and you answered with quiet strength: 'Yes, we can.' But what I truly hope people remember from this night is that this is not merely a victory for African Americans — it is a victory for democracy itself. It signals that America can rise above its divisions. We are witnessing a metamorphosis: voters now honor experience, yet they crave change. I pray we can blend the best of our diverse perspectives to elect a president who embodies our highest ideals. Last night proved we’ve moved beyond business as usual. I congratulate not only Senator Obama, but the entire nation — for shattering a past too often defined by separation, and choosing instead a voice of unity. The victory belongs not just to him, but to everyone who lifted the national conversation above petty racism, outdated political tactics, and fear-driven campaigns — toward a shared vision of the future. As this election season continues, I earnestly hope we resist sinking back into the old patterns of division and pettiness that have haunted us for too long. I am deeply grateful to Senator Hillary Clinton. Through her campaign, my daughters saw that their femininity is not a liability — it is power. Both my sons and daughters now understand: in progressive America, ethnicity is no barrier to greatness. For me, it felt like déjà vu. More than 40 years ago, I watched Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s speeches with my father. Last night, I watched history again — this time with my youngest son. Together, we saw the dreams of enslaved ancestors fulfilled as descendants of both slaves and slaveholders stood together, applauding as one. As I drifted off to sleep, all I could see was the sparkle in my son’s eyes — illuminated by possibility. His heart was full of the belief that, for any qualified, capable person — prepared intellectually and guided by moral conviction — anything is within reach. Congratulations, Senator Obama.

article_content: Washington (CNN) — The Senate Foreign Relations Committee passed a joint resolution Tuesday supporting the limited use of U.S. military force in Libya for one year — a move sought by the Obama administration as it seeks clear congressional backing for its controversial military mission in North Africa. The resolution, which explicitly prohibits the introduction of U.S. ground troops, was approved 14–5 and now moves to the full Senate, which is controlled by Democrats. The Republican-controlled House of Representatives rejected a similar measure last Friday, though it also voted down a bill that would have restricted U.S. involvement in the conflict. Deep divisions in Congress over the mission stem partly from concerns that the White House violated the War Powers Resolution of 1973 — a law requiring presidential notification and congressional approval within 60 days of deploying forces into hostilities, with a 30-day grace period to withdraw. That 90-day window expired last week without congressional authorization for the U.S. role in the NATO-led operation. Administration officials maintain that U.S. actions in Libya — primarily air and drone strikes — do not meet the legal definition of 'hostilities' under the law. President Obama reportedly overruled contrary legal advice from both the Pentagon and the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel in deciding not to seek formal congressional authorization. Earlier Tuesday, Harold Koh, the State Department’s top legal adviser, told the committee that the War Powers Resolution does not apply because the U.S. role is narrowly defined: limited in scope, duration, force exposure, and risk of escalation. 'The precedent here has been narrowly drawn,' Koh asserted. Republicans on the committee disagreed. Senator Richard Lugar of Indiana, the panel’s top Republican, called the president’s decision a 'fundamental failure of leadership that placed expediency before constitutional responsibility.' 'There was no good reason why President Obama should have failed to seek authorization from Congress,' Lugar added, accusing the administration of a 'lack of constitutional discipline.' Senator Bob Corker of Tennessee told Koh he was 'sticking a stick in the eyes of Congress' and had 'undermined the integrity of the War Powers Act.' 'By refusing to take a tougher stance against the administration’s actions,' Corker warned, 'we are making ourselves irrelevant to debates over military engagement.' Koh countered that the law’s automatic termination clause after 60 days — absent explicit congressional approval — is a 'major structural flaw.' 'You cannot run these things by autopilot,' he said, emphasizing the need for executive and legislative judgment in each case. Both Democrats and Republicans acknowledged that the War Powers Resolution is outdated, particularly in light of modern warfare tools like unmanned drone strikes, which were nonexistent in 1973. 'The language needs further clarification,' said Senator John Kerry, the committee’s chairman. However, Kerry warned that Congress pulling out of the mission now would have 'far-reaching consequences' for America’s NATO allies. The NATO-led military operation in Libya, backed by a United Nations mandate, began to protect civilians from violence unleashed by longtime leader Moammar Gadhafi. Western leaders have indicated the mission cannot succeed without Gadhafi’s removal. While the White House has pledged not to deploy U.S. ground troops, bipartisan opposition to the campaign has grown over recent weeks.
translated_content: Washington (CNN) — Le Comité des relations étrangères du Sénat a adopté mardi une résolution conjointe soutenant l'utilisation limitée de la force militaire américaine en Libye pour un an — une initiative demandée par l'administration Obama dans sa quête d'un soutien clair du Congrès pour sa mission controversée en Afrique du Nord. La résolution, qui interdit expressément l'introduction de troupes terrestres américaines, a été approuvée par 14 voix contre 5 et passe maintenant au Sénat dans son ensemble, contrôlé par les démocrates. La Chambre des représentants, contrôlée par les républicains, a rejeté une mesure similaire vendredi dernier, bien qu'elle ait également rejeté un projet de loi visant à restreindre la participation américaine au conflit. Les profondes divisions au Congrès sur cette mission proviennent en partie de la préoccupation que la Maison Blanche a violé la Loi sur les pouvoirs de guerre de 1973 — une loi exigeant que le président informe le Congrès et obtienne son approbation dans les 60 jours suivant le déploiement de forces en hostilités, avec une période de grâce de 30 jours pour mettre fin aux opérations. Cette fenêtre de 90 jours a expiré la semaine dernière sans autorisation explicite du Congrès pour le rôle américain dans l'opération menée par l'OTAN. Les responsables de l'administration affirment que les actions américaines en Libye — principalement des frappes aériennes et des drones — ne répondent pas à la définition légale de 'hostilités' selon la loi. Le président Obama aurait rejeté des avis juridiques contraires provenant à la fois du Pentagone et du Bureau de la conseillère juridique du Département de la Justice en décidant de ne pas solliciter une autorisation formelle du Congrès. Mardi matin, Harold Koh, le principal conseiller juridique du Département d'État, a déclaré au comité que la Loi sur les pouvoirs de guerre ne s'applique pas car le rôle américain est clairement limité : en portée, durée, exposition des forces et risque d'escalade. 'Le précédent ici a été étroitement défini,' a affirmé Koh. Les républicains du comité n'étaient pas d'accord. Le sénateur Richard Lugar de l'Indiana, chef de la majorité républicaine au comité, a qualifié la décision du président de 'défaillance fondamentale du leadership qui a placé l'opportunité avant la responsabilité constitutionnelle.' 'Il n'y avait aucune bonne raison pour que le président Obama n'ait pas cherché d'autorisation du Congrès,' a ajouté Lugar, accusant l'administration de 'manque de discipline constitutionnelle.' Le sénateur Bob Corker du Tennessee a dit à Koh qu'il 'mettait un bâton dans les yeux du Congrès' et avait 'sous-miné l'intégrité de la Loi sur les pouvoirs de guerre.' 'En refusant de prendre une position plus ferme contre les actions de l'administration,' a averti Corker, 'nous nous rendons irrélevants dans les débats sur les actions militaires.' Koh a répliqué que la clause de cessation automatique après 60 jours — en l'absence d'approbation explicite du Congrès — constitue une 'faille structurelle majeure.' 'Vous ne pouvez pas gérer ces choses en mode automatique,' a-t-il dit, soulignant la nécessité d'un jugement exécutif et législatif dans chaque cas. Les démocrates comme les républicains ont reconnu que la Loi sur les pouvoirs de guerre est obsolète, notamment en raison des outils modernes de guerre comme les drones non pilotés, inexistants en 1973. 'Le langage doit être clarifié davantage,' a déclaré le sénateur John Kerry, président du comité. Cependant, Kerry a averti que retirer le Congrès de la mission maintenant aurait des 'conséquences à long terme' pour les alliés de l'OTAN. L'opération militaire menée par l'OTAN en Libye, soutenue par un mandat des Nations Unies, a été lancée pour protéger les civils contre la violence déclenchée par le dirigeant de longue date Mouammar Kadhafi. Les dirigeants occidentaux ont indiqué que la mission ne peut réussir sans la chute de Kadhafi. Bien que la Maison Blanche se soit engagée à ne pas déployer de troupes terrestres américaines, l'opposition bipartite à la campagne a augmenté au cours des dernières semaines.

article_content: The official body responsible for correcting miscarriages of justice, the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), is launching an urgent 'fast-track' inquiry into Wales’s worst mass murder, following a Mail on Sunday investigation. A CCRC spokesperson revealed last night that the case of David Morris, 52, has been granted its highest priority status. Morris is serving four life sentences for the 1999 murders of Mandy Power, 34, her daughters Katie, 10, and Emily, 8, and her 80-year-old mother, Doris Dawson, at their home in Clydach, near Swansea. Mandy Power, a divorcee, was Morris’s occasional lover but was also in a lesbian relationship with Alison Lewis, a former police officer married to Stephen Lewis, a serving South Wales sergeant. Stephen and Alison Lewis were arrested and interviewed early in the investigation but were never charged. Stephen’s twin brother, Inspector Stuart Lewis, was the first senior officer to arrive at the crime scene. After lying in wait and attacking the victims with a heavy pole, the killer set fire to the house to conceal the crime. Inspector Lewis could not account for his movements during the critical hours of June 26, 1999, and delayed reporting the incident as a mass murder and arson. An official inquiry later found he had lied multiple times and he was formally disciplined, though not criminally prosecuted. As revealed last month by the Mail on Sunday, a dossier compiled by Morris’s legal team — Maslen Merchant and QC Francis FitzGibbon — contains compelling new evidence uncovered after a five-year investigation by Brian Thornton, a journalism lecturer at Winchester University. The dossier includes a recorded message from a trusted police informant stating that Mandy Power had been threatened by 'her current lover’s husband, who was a police officer.' Forensic tests conducted before Morris’s trial detected male DNA on the murder weapon, matches used to start the fire, and on Mandy’s clothing and watch. However, no follow-up tests were performed to determine if this DNA matched Morris or another individual. Morris, imprisoned at Long Lartin in Worcestershire, has consistently maintained his innocence and is urging the CCRC to conduct these missing tests immediately. Following the Mail on Sunday report, several new witnesses have come forward with potentially crucial information, all of which will now be examined as part of the CCRC’s renewed inquiry.

Un porte-parole de la CCRC a révélé hier soir que l'affaire de David Morris, 52 ans, a reçu le statut de priorité maximale. Morris purge quatre peines de réclusion à perpétuité pour les meurtres de Mandy Power, 34 ans, ses filles Katie, 10 ans, et Emily, 8 ans, ainsi que sa mère de 80 ans, Doris Dawson, commis en 1999 dans leur domicile de Clydach, près de Swansea. Mandy Power, divorcée, était une amante occasionnelle de Morris, mais entretenait également une relation lesbienne avec Alison Lewis, une ancienne policière mariée à Stephen Lewis, un sergent en service au Pays de Galles du Sud. Stephen et Alison Lewis ont été arrêtés et interrogés au début de l'enquête, mais n'ont jamais été inculpés. Le frère jumeau de Stephen, l'inspecteur Stuart Lewis, a été le premier officier supérieur à arriver sur les lieux du crime. Après avoir attendu dans l'ombre et attaqué les victimes avec une barre lourde, le tueur a mis le feu à la maison pour dissimuler son crime. L'inspecteur Lewis n'a pas pu expliquer ses mouvements pendant les heures critiques du 26 juin 1999 et a retardé le signalement de l'incident comme un meurtre de masse et un incendie criminel. Une enquête officielle a ultérieurement révélé qu'il avait menti à plusieurs reprises et il a été formellement sanctionné, bien qu'il n'ait pas été poursuivi pénalement. Comme révélé le mois dernier par le Mail on Sunday, un dossier compilé par l'équipe juridique de Morris — Maslen Merchant et l'avocat Francis FitzGibbon — contient de nouvelles preuves convaincantes découvertes après cinq années d'enquête menées par Brian Thornton, enseignant en journalisme à l'université de Winchester. Le dossier inclut un enregistrement d'un message provenant d'un informateur fiable de la police, affirmant que Mandy Power avait été menacée par 'l'époux de son amant actuel, qui était un policier.' Des tests médico-légaux réalisés avant le procès de Morris ont détecté des traces d'ADN masculin sur l'arme du meurtre, les allumettes utilisées pour allumer le feu, ainsi que sur les vêtements et la montre de Mandy. Toutefois, aucune analyse complémentaire n'a été effectuée pour déterminer si cet ADN correspondait à Morris ou à une autre personne. Morris, incarcéré à Long Lartin dans le Worcestershire, affirme constamment son innocence et demande à la CCRC d'effectuer ces tests manquants dès que possible. Suite au rapport du Mail on Sunday, plusieurs nouveaux témoins se sont présentés avec des informations potentiellement cruciales, qui seront désormais examinées dans le cadre de la nouvelle enquête de la CCRC.

article_content: CNN) — Robin Stearns, 28, watched her husband apply for jobs day after day. She saw him scour professional networking sites, trying to connect with potential employers. Frustrated by the lack of responses, she decided to make him stand out: she created a website dedicated to helping him find work. Using her tax refund, she bought a MacBook, which included built-in website-building tools. Within days, myhusbandneedsajob.com went live. "I grew frustrated," said Robin, a resident of San Francisco, California. "He’s been sending out resumes since he graduated, but nothing’s happened. He’s an outstanding candidate — he’d be an asset to any company." Michael Stearns, 30, earned his Master of Business Administration from Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., in May 2008. He is seeking a role in corporate marketing but remains open to other reasonable opportunities. The website features a photo of Robin holding a sign that reads, 'My husband needs a job.' It also displays Michael’s resume, a profile interview, and additional details. As the economy struggles and unemployment rises, job seekers are turning to creativity to capture attention. Paul Forster, co-founder and CEO of Indeed.com, encourages candidates to differentiate themselves instead of flooding the market with generic applications. 'Don’t resort to the shotgun approach,' he advises. The internet has become a vital tool for job seekers. Platforms like Twitter and Facebook host public groups sharing job leads, while blogs offer emotional support and practical advice, reminding people they’re not alone. For the Stearnses, breaking from conventional tactics appears to be working. In just three days, the site received dozens of emails from employers and others facing similar challenges. Michael plans to follow up on these leads. According to the U.S. Department of Labor, California’s unemployment rate stands at 10.1%, among the highest in the nation, compared to the national average of 8.1%. Robin, who declined to discuss her own employment to keep focus on her husband’s search, noted that nearly 90% of their friends have been affected by layoffs. The couple intends to keep the site active for now. 'At least until I get a job,' Michael said.

article_content: For decades, the United Nations successfully banned smoking within its walls — now, officials are turning their attention to another habit: drinking. U.S. Ambassador Joseph Torsella, known for pushing management reforms, recently issued a rare public rebuke targeting alcohol use during critical negotiations. Speaking to the Fifth Committee — the body responsible for budgets and administration — he urged that meeting rooms become 'inebriation-free zones' moving forward. According to U.S. diplomats, late-night sessions, especially around the holiday season, have seen increased alcohol consumption, with some delegates allegedly bringing liquor into the building since the UN’s main bar closed in 2010 due to renovations. While no nation was singled out, Russian Ambassador Vitaly Churkin acknowledged the issue, promising to instruct his delegation to abstain from drinking during official work hours. Not everyone agrees there’s a problem. British Ambassador Mark Lyall Grant noted that while diplomatic receptions often include drinks, alcohol has never interfered with actual negotiations. Others pointed out that the UN complex, once home to a delegates’ lounge with a bar, now offers limited food and beverage options after 3 p.m., possibly encouraging discreet consumption. The UN Secretariat, through spokesperson Eduardo Del Buey, declined to enforce rules on member states, stating that behavioral norms fall under national jurisdiction. The reference to a 2011 incident — where former UN official Sha Zukang drunkenly insulted then-Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon at a dinner — served as a cautionary tale, though officials emphasized that such episodes are isolated. Torsella, who has also criticized lavish business-class travel, added: 'Let’s save the champagne for celebrating success — not during the work itself.' When asked about post-meeting drinking, Churkin simply smiled: 'After hours? That’s personal. We all have our private lives.'

article_content: The Christian Science Monitor recently reported that Mitt Romney’s former political advisers are firmly denying rumors that he might run for president in 2016. 'I take Mitt at his absolute word,' said Ron Kaufman. 'He’s not running.' Whether Romney wants to run—or whether his family supports such a move—is ultimately up to him. But if he does decide to enter the race, it’s not unreasonable to imagine him securing the Republican nomination in 2016. Most pundits assumed his political career was over after his 2012 defeat to President Obama. Yet a sympathetic portrayal in the Netflix documentary 'Mitt,' coupled with his active fundraising for 2014 midterm candidates, has reignited speculation. The odds remain slim. Republicans may hesitate to nominate someone who failed to win the 2008 primary and then lost decisively to Obama. Many viewed Obama as a one-term president—akin to Jimmy Carter—but Democrats successfully painted Romney as out-of-touch, focused solely on the wealthy and lacking authenticity. Yet history offers examples of political comebacks. After losing to John F. Kennedy in 1960 and to Pat Brown in the 1962 California gubernatorial race, Richard Nixon declared, 'You won’t have Nixon to kick around anymore.' He was wrong—not because he disappeared, but because he returned stronger in 1968, rebuilding his image as a statesman and winning the presidency against Hubert Humphrey. Similarly, Ronald Reagan, after narrowly losing the 1976 Republican nomination to Gerald Ford, spent the next four years refining his message through weekly radio broadcasts. By 1980, he was the frontrunner—and defeated Jimmy Carter. Like Nixon in 1966, Romney has remained active on the campaign trail in 2014. He is, as one Republican consultant told CNN, 'the man in demand'—a star attraction at fundraising events. Other potential GOP contenders face serious drawbacks: Senator Rand Paul’s libertarianism alienates mainstream conservatives; New Jersey Governor Chris Christie’s reputation remains damaged by 'Bridgegate'; Wisconsin’s Scott Walker faces his own controversies; Florida’s Marco Rubio struggles to reconcile his immigrant-friendly stance with the party’s hardline immigration position; former Florida Governor Jeb Bush must overcome lingering public resentment over his brother’s presidency; and Wisconsin Representative Paul Ryan, while increasingly plausible, is seen as too closely tied to the party’s far-right wing, which polls poorly. Despite criticism of Romney’s wealth and economic record, his advocacy for deregulation and tax cuts aligns perfectly with the GOP’s core agenda since Reagan. The party’s central focus has long been shrinking government oversight of the economy—not social issues. On these grounds, Romney retains strong appeal among major donors and conservative activists—including the Koch brothers—as the candidate best positioned to advance their economic priorities. Money and endorsements matter significantly. It is not far-fetched to envision Mitt Romney leading the Republican ticket in 2016. Whether he could defeat Hillary Clinton or another Democratic nominee remains uncertain—but his potential candidacy is far from implausible.

article_content: As the 2012 Olympics approach, Heathrow Airport is grappling with worsening immigration delays due to the deployment of hundreds of undertrained staff, according to John Vine, the independent chief inspector of borders and immigration. These temporary workers — many with no prior immigration experience — are reportedly slowing down passenger processing, asking fewer follow-up questions, and increasing wait times despite efforts to reduce queues. To cope with projected daily passenger surges exceeding 100,000, the UK Border Force has rehired retired officers and reassigned staff from other departments. However, inspections reveal that these personnel lack confidence and operational proficiency, leading to inefficiencies at primary control points. Discrepancies in forged document detection between terminals are also concerning: Terminal 4 detected 275 forgeries between April 2010 and March 2012, compared to just 177 in Terminal 3. Staff attribute part of this gap to malfunctioning detection equipment in Terminal 3. While the Border Force claims improvements — including a central control room, revised operating mandates, and ongoing recruitment — critics argue these measures are short-term fixes masking deeper structural failures. Shadow Home Secretary Yvette Cooper condemned the rehiring of former staff as a 'damning admission' of past cuts, noting nearly 900 border officers were dismissed since the last election. Labour’s Keith Vaz warned that placing inadequately trained personnel at critical checkpoints during such a high-profile event is 'unacceptable.' Meanwhile, Immigration Minister Damian Green avoided committing to maintaining full staffing levels after the Games, stating only that staffing will be adjusted dynamically based on passenger flow.
