article_content: After eight decades in obscurity, Oswald the Lucky Rabbit — the forgotten predecessor to Mickey Mouse — is finally stepping back into the spotlight. Disney has reignited interest in the character, featuring him alongside Mickey in the upcoming video game 'Epic Mickey 2: The Power of Two' and unveiling a rare 1928 sketch by Walt Disney himself for a new exhibition. The pencil sketch, drawn for the 1928 animated short 'Sky Scrappers,' depicts Oswald shielding himself from falling bricks with an umbrella. Found in the 1970s and preserved in Disney’s archives ever since, it’s now being showcased as part of the game’s promotional campaign. Warren Spector, creative director at Junction Point Studios, expressed excitement about reintroducing Oswald to modern audiences: 'It’s amazing. Everyone at Disney is proud he’s back. To have Mickey and Oswald united to save the world? It’s unbelievable.' Oswald was originally created in 1926 while Walt Disney worked under contract with Universal. But in 1928, after Disney requested a budget increase, distributor Charles Mintz — who owned the character — demanded a 20% pay cut and secretly hired away Disney’s entire animation team. Disney refused and produced his final Oswald cartoons under protest. Devastated but determined, Disney vowed never again to lose control of his creations. Inspired by a pet mouse from his childhood, he and animator Ub Iwerks developed a new character. Originally named 'Mortimer Mouse,' the character was renamed 'Mickey Mouse' at the suggestion of Walt’s wife, Lillian. For decades, Oswald remained out of Disney’s hands — until 2006, when CEO Bob Iger brokered a landmark deal with NBCUniversal, trading sportscaster Al Michaels for the rights to Oswald and several other classic characters. Archivist Becky Cline noted that many early Oswald drawings were lost or discarded during Disney’s 1939 studio relocation to Burbank, making the surviving sketches invaluable. 'We always loved him,' she said. 'But he didn’t belong to us — until now.' With his return, Oswald symbolizes both a corporate triumph and a cultural reclamation — reminding fans that behind every iconic mouse lies a rabbit who almost vanished from history.

article_content: Bestselling author John Grisham has publicly apologized after remarks he made in a British newspaper interview sparked national outrage. During the conversation promoting his novel Gray Mountain, Grisham suggested that many men serving time for possessing child pornography were not violent predators but rather ordinary middle-aged men who accidentally stumbled upon illegal content — possibly after drinking — by clicking the wrong links online. He described U.S. prisons as overcrowded with 'guys my age,' emphasizing that these individuals had never physically harmed a child. While acknowledging that those who exploit children should face severe consequences, Grisham argued that the legal system had become excessive in its punishments. His comments, which drew sharp criticism from child protection groups, implied a distinction between 'real pedophiles' and those he viewed as unintentional offenders. Following intense public backlash, including condemnation from organizations like the NSPCC, Grisham issued a formal apology. He clarified that his words were never intended to minimize the suffering of victims or show sympathy for offenders. 'I can think of nothing more despicable than exploiting children,' he wrote. 'I deeply regret making those remarks and offer my sincere apologies.'

article_content: In early March 2023, South Africa began culling millions of chickens to stop the spread of two dangerous strains of avian flu. By Tuesday, officials confirmed that roughly 7.5 million birds—both meat and egg-laying chickens—had been destroyed across the country. This drastic move came after more than 60 outbreaks were recorded, with over half concentrated in Gauteng, home to Johannesburg and Pretoria. Many grocery stores in Johannesburg responded by limiting customers to one carton of six eggs per person, as egg supplies dwindled. The government admitted that food supply chains were under strain. According to the South African Poultry Association, the culls included about 2.5 million broiler chickens and 5 million layers, representing 20–30% of the nation’s total chicken population. To prevent further shortages, Agriculture Minister Thoko Didiza announced plans to speed up import permits for eggs from abroad. Officials are also evaluating a vaccination campaign, though vaccines won’t be available for at least two to six months. Meanwhile, Namibia has shut its borders to South African poultry products. The outbreak comes on top of an ongoing electricity crisis: frequent blackouts have already forced farmers to cull nearly 10 million young chicks earlier this year due to overheating and overcrowding. Industry leaders say the current crisis is the worst in recent memory, with losses already exceeding $25 million. Wilhelm Mare of the South African Veterinary Association warned that up to 8.5 million laying hens could be lost, with total bird deaths possibly reaching 10 million. He called the situation 'catastrophic.' Globally, the U.S. CDC reported over 21,000 avian flu outbreaks since 2013, though human infections remain rare. For South Africans, eggs are a vital, low-cost protein—and with inflation already high, prices are expected to climb even further. Adding to tensions, poultry producers are urging the government to impose long-term tariffs on cheap imports from Brazil, the U.S., Poland, Denmark, and Spain, claiming these imports undermine local farmers.

article_content: The mother of British man Grant Cameron has described his alleged torture by Dubai police, as the trio of UK citizens—Cameron, Suneet Jeerh, and Karl Williams—await a verdict in their drug trial. All three deny charges of possessing and intending to distribute synthetic cannabis, known as 'spice,' which police claim was found in their car during a vacation in August 2012. Tracy Cameron recounted a harrowing account of her son’s detention: he and his companions were reportedly beaten, isolated, and subjected to electric shocks—including to sensitive areas—while blindfolded and threatened with death. They were also pressured to sign confessions in Arabic, a language none understood. Amid growing international attention, UK Prime Minister David Cameron voiced 'concern' over the case during a state visit by the UAE president, urging an independent investigation and highlighting the absence of medical examinations. The Foreign Office confirmed it has raised the matter with senior Emirati officials. Human rights organization Reprieve has called for the charges to be dropped and the men released, citing credible evidence of abuse documented by UK consular staff. However, UAE academic Dr. Abdul-Kallek Abdulla dismissed the claims as unfounded, asserting that such practices are inconsistent with UAE law and official policy. If convicted, the men could face minimum sentences of 15 years. Their trial began in February 2013, following seven months in pre-trial detention.

article_content: In September, Somalia took a historic leap toward peace by electing its first president on home soil in over 20 years. Hassan Sheikh Mohamud — a university professor, longtime activist, and former UN staffer — was inaugurated in Mogadishu after narrowly defeating outgoing President Sheikh Sharif Sheikh Ahmed. The vote, widely praised by global observers, signaled a fragile but real improvement in security after decades of brutal conflict. Still, Mohamud inherits a nation in ruins: infrastructure is shattered, the economy is in freefall, and vast regions remain under the grip of armed groups like Al-Shabaab, linked to al-Qaeda. Though militants have retreated from the capital, their presence elsewhere keeps the country far from secure. Professor Ahmed Ismail Samatar, a respected scholar and former presidential contender now serving in parliament, describes the task ahead as immense. 'He truly cares about Somalia,' Samatar says. 'There’s a chance his leadership can pivot us toward the future we’ve been waiting for.' Samatar reminds us that Somalia wasn’t always broken. In the 1960s, shortly after gaining independence from Britain and Italy, it became the first sub-Saharan African nation to peacefully transfer power through a transparent parliamentary election — a rare democratic milestone. That changed in 1969 when President Shermarke was assassinated, triggering a military takeover that lasted two decades. After dictator Siyaad Barre was ousted in 1991, chaos took root and never fully left. 'No African country has fallen so far since independence,' Samatar notes. Yet today, he sees glimmers of change. After 30 years of research and witnessing suffering firsthand, he believes Somalis are done with warlords, extremists, and endless bloodshed. 'They’re exhausted,' he says. 'And exhaustion is breeding something powerful — a quiet, collective hunger for something better.' Now back at Macalester College in Minnesota — home to one of the largest Somali diasporas in the U.S. — Samatar continues to fight for his homeland, not just as a professor, but as a legislator.

article_content: Going food shopping with your mother was only ever truly fun if you could ride along in the cart—and the animal kingdom is no different, as these anteaters show. An exhausted baby giant anteater climbed onto its mother’s back for a much-needed rest as the hunt for food became too taxing. The tiny animal slumped against its mother while she dug through the soil in search of ants and termites. The unusual creatures were photographed in the Pantanal wetlands of western Brazil. The giant anteater, also known as the ant bear due to its large size, is found across Central and South America. Young anteaters commonly ride on their mothers’ backs, using their long claws to grip the thick fur—where they are cleverly camouflaged from predators. The one-foot-long baby anteater was dwarfed by its mother, which measured nearly nine feet from nose to tail. The pair were captured by Mario Haberfeld, a 37-year-old former racing driver who now leads a jaguar conservation project. Haberfeld was visiting the region with his son when they encountered the pair. Giant anteaters have poor eyesight; as long as you remain upwind, you can approach them closely. Haberfeld said: 'We slowly walked over until we were about six feet away. They are very docile creatures and simply carried on foraging.' Giant anteaters have long nails and thick fur, allowing babies to easily climb aboard for rest. Haberfeld added: 'I’ve been coming to this region for ten years—sights like this are common. As long as the babies are small, mothers are happy to carry them.' The giant anteater is the largest of the four anteater species and possesses one of the longest tongues relative to body size in the animal kingdom—measuring over two feet. Native to Central and South America, they inhabit diverse ecosystems including grasslands, savannas, and rainforests. Baby anteaters typically remain with their mothers until they are nine or ten months old, after which they become independent.

article_content: Somewhere buried on his iPhone camera roll is a photograph Ed Woodward took of the scoreboard after Manchester United lost 2-0 to Olympiakos in the Champions League last season. Caught at the Karaiskakis Stadium, the United chief executive, arm outstretched, looked almost like a fan—or a tourist. But Woodward took that photo for a reason. It was the night he and other members of the United board realized David Moyes was no longer the right man for the club. Woodward saw players going through the motions, surrendering to what was arguably the weakest team still in the competition. Fresh ideas: Louis van Gaal brings an 'aura' to Manchester United, and Ed Woodward believes he is the right man for the job. Learning on the job: United CEO Ed Woodward (left) says he is adapting to his role. VIDEO: United will continue to spend—Woodward. In the spotlight: Van Gaal is interviewed by MUTV as he prepares for his first game in charge. New man: Van Gaal (right) will bring fresh ideas; here he speaks with David Beckham (left) and Ryan Giggs. New era: Van Gaal is determined to restore success at Manchester United. As such, he took the photograph as a personal reminder of how low the club had fallen—a visual anchor to look back on when things improved. Ahead of Louis van Gaal’s first game as United manager at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena tonight, Woodward is convinced things are about to get significantly better. 'As I look back, I feel far more positivity for this coming season,' Woodward said last night. 'Part of that is because of what Louis achieved at the World Cup. It’s restored a sense of pride around the club. He’s impressed everyone since arriving. There’s real energy and buzz here.' If last season was difficult for Moyes and United—who finished seventh in the Premier League—it was also tough for Woodward. Many perceived him as a novice CEO struggling in the transfer market. He was mocked on social media and heavily criticized in the press. While Moyes operated in the shadow of Sir Alex Ferguson, Woodward faced similar comparisons to his predecessor, David Gill. The 42-year-old admits his quest for credibility continues. 'It was a challenging year,' he said, with understatement. 'Ideally, I would’ve worked alongside Alex for a year. I would’ve loved that. Most of the job wasn’t surprising—I’ve been at the club for nine years—but I didn’t walk in knowing everything. Credibility comes with time and experience. I wouldn’t expect fans to give it to me on day one.' 'Criticism comes with the job. With long-term plans, you can’t be distracted by short-term noise. I’m still learning—and I welcome feedback. Listening to fans is essential.' Speaking at United’s hotel in Beverly Hills this week, Woodward delayed his return to England to honor media commitments. To him, perception matters—not out of vanity, but because he recognizes that United’s public image has often suffered. Early signs suggest van Gaal—whose side faces LA Galaxy today—has already lifted morale at Old Trafford. While there’s been criticism of the training facilities (remedial work began yesterday), staff describe a coach energized—not intimidated—by the challenge. 'We’re a different class of club,' Woodward said. 'No one truly understands what it means to manage Manchester United until they’ve done it. But Louis is clearly excited by it.' 'He was one of the most proactive managers at the World Cup—he made bold decisions on the pitch. That raised his profile, and it helps us.' Woodward’s stance on transfer spending is clear: if van Gaal needs funds, he’ll get them. He won’t discuss breaking records—knowing headlines follow—but pointed to last week’s £750 million kit deal with Adidas as proof of the club’s financial power and global stature. 'As Louis put it eloquently, seventh place last year isn’t acceptable. But this deal—and everything we’re doing commercially, from agent talks to attracting players—confirms one thing: we are the biggest club in the world. No question in my mind.' 'The truth is, we’re not afraid to spend big in the transfer market. Whether it’s a record or not doesn’t matter to us. There’s no budget. We’re in a very strong financial position. We can make major signings.'

'En regardant en arrière, je ressens bien plus de positivité pour cette saison à venir,' a déclaré Woodward hier soir. 'Cela vient en partie de ce que Louis a accompli à la Coupe du monde. Cela a redonné une fierté au club. Il a impressionné tout le monde depuis son arrivée. Il y a vraiment de l'énergie et de l'enthousiasme ici.' Si la saison dernière a été difficile pour Moyes et Manchester United — qui ont terminé septièmes en Premier League — elle ne l'a pas été non plus pour Woodward. Beaucoup le perçoivent comme un PDG novice ayant du mal à conclure des transferts. Il a été moqué sur les réseaux sociaux et vivement critiqué dans les médias traditionnels. Alors que Moyes opérait sous l'ombre de Sir Alex Ferguson, Woodward a subi des comparaisons similaires avec son prédécesseur, David Gill. L'homme de 42 ans admet que sa quête de crédibilité continue. 'C'était une année difficile,' a-t-il dit, avec une certaine retenue. 'Idéalement, j'aurais aimé travailler aux côtés d'Alex pendant un an. J'aurais adoré cela. La plupart du travail n'était pas une surprise — je suis au club depuis neuf ans — mais je n'ai pas atterri en sachant tout. La crédibilité vient avec le temps et l'expérience. Je ne peux pas attendre que les supporters me la donnent dès le premier jour.' 'La critique fait partie du métier. Avec des projets à long terme, vous ne pouvez pas vous laisser distraire par les problèmes à court terme. J'apprends encore — et j'apprécie les retours. Écouter les supporters est essentiel.' Parlant à l'hôtel du club à Beverly Hills cette semaine, Woodward a repoussé son vol de retour en Angleterre pour honorer ses engagements médiatiques. Pour lui, la perception compte — pas par vanité personnelle, mais parce qu'il reconnaît que l'image publique de Manchester United n'a pas toujours été excellente. Les premiers signes indiquent que van Gaal — dont l'équipe affronte LA Galaxy aujourd'hui — a déjà redonné du moral à Old Trafford. Bien qu'il y ait eu des critiques sur les installations d'entraînement (des travaux de rénovation ont commencé hier matin), le personnel du club décrit un entraîneur énergisé — et non intimidé — par le défi. 'Nous sommes un club d'une autre envergure,' a déclaré Woodward. 'Personne ne comprend vraiment ce que signifie entraîner Manchester United avant d'avoir été manager de Manchester United. Mais Louis est clairement enthousiasmé par cela.' 'Il était l'un des entraîneurs les plus proactifs à la Coupe du monde — il a pris des décisions audacieuses sur le terrain. Cela a renforcé son profil, et cela nous aide.' La position de Woodward sur les dépenses de transfert est claire : si van Gaal a besoin d'argent, il peut l'avoir. Il ne veut pas parler de records de transfert — il connaît les titres qui suivent — mais il a souligné l'accord récent avec Adidas pour un contrat de 750 millions de livres sterling comme preuve de la puissance financière et du statut mondial du club. 'Comme Louis l'a dit avec éloquence, septième place l'année dernière n'est pas acceptable. Mais cet accord — et tout ce que nous faisons sur le plan commercial, des négociations avec les agents à l'attraction des joueurs — confirme une chose : nous sommes le plus grand club du monde. Aucun doute à ce sujet.' 'La réalité est que nous n'avons pas peur de dépenser de grosses sommes sur le marché des transferts. Que ce soit un record ou non ne nous intéresse pas vraiment. Il n'y a pas de budget. Nous sommes dans une très bonne position financière. Nous pouvons faire de gros achats.'

article_content: Justine Sacco found herself trending worldwide on Twitter after posting an ill-considered message meant to be humorous. A PR consultant later revealed how a tweet intended to amuse her 170 followers turned her into a global target of hatred — and destroyed her career and personal life. In December 2013, just before boarding a flight to South Africa, Sacco, a 30-year-old from New York, tweeted: 'Going to Africa. Hope I don't get AIDS. Just kidding. I'm white!' The tweet was retweeted by tech blogger Sam Biddle to his 15,000 followers, sparking widespread outrage. Thousands accused her of racism and ignorance, demanding her dismissal as Senior Director of Corporate Communications at IAC. Unaware of the backlash due to her phone being off during her 11-hour flight, Sacco had no idea that her employer had issued a statement calling the comment 'outrageous and offensive' and noting she was 'currently unreachable on an incoming flight.' The hashtag #HasJustineLandedYet began trending globally as people eagerly awaited her reaction. A friend deleted her Twitter account, but the damage was irreversible. She was fired, and public humiliation persisted. BuzzFeed later published an article titled '16 Tweets Justine Sacco Regrets,' dredging up old posts. More than a year later, Sacco spoke with bestselling British author Jon Ronson for his book, So You've Been Publicly Shamed. She explained she never intended the tweet to be taken literally: 'Only an insane person would think white people don’t get AIDS.' She added, 'I thought there was no way anyone could possibly interpret it as serious.' Sacco admitted deep regret: 'Unfortunately, I’m not a character on South Park or a comedian — I had no business making such a politically incorrect joke on a public platform.' She described her tweet as satire targeting the cultural ignorance common among Americans: 'Living in America puts us in a bubble about the rest of the world. I was mocking that bubble.' Ronson, known for books like The Men Who Stare at Goats and The Psychopath Test, used Sacco’s case to explore how social media has transformed public shaming into a mass spectacle. He wrote in the New York Times: 'Shame campaigns now target not just powerful institutions, but ordinary people for minor transgressions — and the punishment often far exceeds the offense.' Sacco described the emotional toll: 'I cried out my body weight in the first 24 hours. I couldn’t sleep. I’d wake up in the middle of the night, disoriented.' Her career, relationships, and mental health were shattered. 'I’m single now — I can’t date because people Google everyone. That part of my life is gone too.' She eventually resolved to rebuild: 'I couldn’t sit at home watching movies and crying forever. I had to reclaim my identity.' Today, she has a new job and avoids social media. She told Ronson she will not speak publicly about the incident again — 'Anything that puts the spotlight on me is negative.' Ronson compares modern online shaming to historical public floggings, arguing that the real driver is not justice, but attention-seeking. 'Her tormentors were rewarded for tearing her down — just as she had sought approval through her tweet. Both were chasing validation from strangers.' So You've Been Publicly Shamed, published by Picador on March 12, 2015, urges readers to reflect on the cruelty and impulsivity of digital mob justice.

article_content: By Suzannah Hills. Cuba's reclusive former president, Fidel Castro, has been photographed in public for the first time in nearly a year. The revolutionary leader attended the inauguration of an art gallery in Havana, run by Cuban artist Alexis Leyva — known as Kcho — yesterday. It marks his first public appearance since attending a National Assembly meeting in February 2013. Photographs show the 87-year-old Castro seated, wearing a blue sweatshirt, and looking intently at an artwork while being assisted by an aide and a metal walking stick. Castro, who relinquished power to his brother Raúl Castro in 2008 after suffering serious intestinal bleeding in 2006, has maintained a low profile in recent years. His absence following the death of Nelson Mandela — a close ally — sparked widespread speculation about his health. Mandela was a longtime supporter of Cuba’s military assistance to Angolan forces fighting apartheid-era South Africa in the 1980s. In early December, Castro met with Spanish journalist Ignacio Ramonet for over two hours. Photos from the meeting, published by Cubadebate, depict Castro engaged in conversation, gesturing with his left hand. Ramonet told the Associated Press that Castro was in 'excellent health' and in 'good spirits, physically, mentally, and psychologically.' They discussed Mandela, Venezuelan politics, and climate change. While Fidel has remained out of the public eye, his brother Raúl has drawn attention through diplomatic actions — notably shaking hands with U.S. President Barack Obama during Mandela’s memorial service in South Africa. That gesture revealed that officials from both nations had already been in secret talks for six months. On Air Force One, Deputy National Security Adviser Ben Rhodes confirmed, 'It’s been quite some time since the presidents of the United States and Cuba were even in the same place.' He added that discussions focused on migration issues, aiming to strengthen ties between Cuban Americans and the island nation. Official photographs of Fidel Castro have been released in recent months to address growing speculation about his condition.

article_content: The U.S. House of Representatives has rejected a bid to censure Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib, the only Palestinian American member of Congress, following intense debate over her advocacy for Palestinian rights during Israel’s war in Gaza. The censure resolution, introduced by far-right Republican Marjorie Taylor Greene, was defeated by a vote of 222 to 186, with 23 Republicans crossing party lines to oppose it. In response, Democratic lawmakers withdrew a separate motion to censure Greene. Greene’s resolution falsely accused Tlaib of 'antisemitic activity,' 'sympathizing with terrorist organizations,' and 'leading an insurrection' at the U.S. Capitol — referencing a peaceful sit-in by Jewish activists demanding a Gaza ceasefire. Tlaib rejected the charges as baseless and politically motivated, calling the resolution 'unhinged,' 'deeply Islamophobic,' and an attack on peaceful Jewish anti-war advocates. Tlaib, a vocal critic of U.S. policy in the region, has consistently demanded an immediate ceasefire, unrestricted humanitarian aid, the release of hostages and detainees, and an end to what she calls Israel’s collective punishment of Palestinians — a violation of international law. She has also criticized President Joe Biden and Secretary Antony Blinken for failing to push for a ceasefire. The war escalated after Hamas launched a deadly attack on southern Israel on October 7, killing more than 1,400 people, according to Israeli officials. Israel’s subsequent military campaign has resulted in over 8,700 Palestinian deaths, per Gaza health authorities. An ongoing Israeli siege has severely restricted access to food, water, fuel, and electricity in Gaza, where hospitals are overwhelmed and civilians face extreme deprivation. Tlaib has urged Americans to witness the suffering in Gaza: 'See what’s happening. Don’t turn away. All they need to do is see Palestinians as human to recognize these are war crimes.' Despite its symbolic nature, the failed censure effort leaves a lasting mark on the political landscape, highlighting deep divisions over human rights, free speech, and U.S. foreign policy.

article_content: At the Cheltenham Literature Festival, former Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams shared a deeply personal appeal: he knows two bishops currently held captive by armed extremists in Syria. Speaking during a discussion on 'Rights, Law and Religion,' Williams urged the West not to look away from the brutal reality facing religious minorities in the region. A member of the audience highlighted the horrific toll — hundreds of Christians, including women and children, buried alive or imprisoned — and asked if silence was no longer an option. Williams responded with conviction: 'I couldn’t agree more.' He stressed that the rise of religious extremism isn’t just a regional crisis but a global warning. Though he didn’t name them, his reference was clearly to Bishop Boulos Yazigi and Bishop John Ibrahim, seized from their vehicle near Aleppo in April 2013. Their driver was killed; the attackers were widely believed to be Chechen militants linked to Jabhat al-Nusra, who targeted them because of their faith and perceived loyalty to the Assad government. Meanwhile, as ISIS surged across northern Syria and Iraq, the Syrian regime capitalized on the chaos, positioning itself as a defender of Christians and other minorities — a narrative that has gained unintended traction internationally. Williams also reflected on religion’s darker chapters, acknowledging that Christianity once justified slavery and other atrocities, yet later became a force for liberation. When pressed on whether the Church of England should lose its official status, he admitted he wouldn’t design the system today — but argued that its presence in Parliament still offers symbolic space for faith voices, even if it feels outdated. 'I’m not in a rush to remove it,' he said. 'It lets others know they, too, belong.'

article_content: If you’ve ever attended a football match, you’re unlikely to be surprised that fans often swear. But a recent study reveals a twist: fans are more likely to direct their profanity at their own team than at referees or opponents. Researchers analyzing tweets during English Premier League matches found that roughly one in every 20 tweets contained a swearword — and Liverpool supporters were among the most frequent offenders. The study, led by Dr. Emma Byrne and Dr. David Corney from Robert Gordon University (RGU), examined over 125,000 tweets per match day across three consecutive Saturday afternoons. Nearly 6,500 tweets — just over 5% — included the two most common English swearwords. Contrary to assumptions, swearing wasn’t solely tied to frustration. Fans used profanity during moments of joy — such as scoring a goal — as well as in humor, irony, and self-deprecation. The researchers concluded that context is critical: swearing can express affection, solidarity, and intense emotional investment — not just anger. 'It’s no secret football fans swear,' said Dr. Byrne, herself a Liverpool supporter. 'But we found they swear even more when something great happens. Even after scoring, Liverpool fans still find something to complain about.' Dr. Corney emphasized the broader implications: 'Sentiment analysis tools have long treated swearing as a clear signal of negativity. Our work shows it’s often an intensifier — used to amplify excitement, pride, or belonging.' The findings, published in the paper 'Sweet FA: sentiment, swearing and soccer,' challenge conventional views of online emotion and suggest that profanity among fans functions as a cultural badge of loyalty and passion.

article_content: In 1972, an 18-year-old Sri Lankan named Velupillai Prabhakaran, deeply disturbed by what he saw as decades of institutional neglect and discrimination against the Tamil minority, picked up a revolver and began organizing what would become one of the most formidable insurgent movements in modern history. His group, the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), grew into a disciplined force that fought for 25 years to establish an independent homeland for Sri Lanka’s Tamil population — a conflict that claimed more than 70,000 lives. Known globally for its ruthless tactics, the LTTE became the first group to widely deploy female suicide bombers and is credited by the FBI with inventing the suicide belt. It also holds the grim distinction of being the only terrorist organization to assassinate two sitting heads of state: India’s Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi in 1991 and Sri Lanka’s President Ranasinghe Premadasa in 1993. After years of brutal warfare, the Sri Lankan military launched a decisive offensive that dismantled the LTTE’s strongholds in the north and east. By late 2009, the rebels, reduced to a small remnant, declared they would lay down their weapons. Shortly after, the Sri Lankan government announced that Prabhakaran had been killed — a moment many hoped would finally bring closure to Asia’s longest-running civil war. The Tamils, making up roughly 12% of Sri Lanka’s 20 million people, are predominantly Hindu and speak Tamil, distinguishing them from the Sinhalese majority, who are Buddhist and speak Sinhala. Historical tensions stem from British colonial policies that favored Tamils in education and administration, fueling resentment among Sinhalese. After independence in 1948, Sinhalese leaders enacted laws that marginalized Tamil political representation, language rights, and employment opportunities. By the 1970s, peaceful Tamil demands for autonomy evolved into calls for full separation — Tamil Eelam. Prabhakaran, operating from hidden jungle bases and famously wearing a cyanide pill to avoid capture, demanded absolute loyalty from his fighters. While the Sri Lankan state branded him a terrorist, many Tamils revered him as their only defender. His legacy remains fiercely contested: a symbol of resistance to some, a butcher to others. The LTTE recruited largely from impoverished Tamil youth who felt excluded from economic opportunity. Though internationally isolated and condemned, the group avoided attacking Western tourists, fearing backlash against Tamil diaspora communities funding their cause. Multiple peace attempts, including a Norwegian-brokered truce in 2002, collapsed amid mutual distrust. In 2008, the Sri Lankan government scrapped the ceasefire and launched a full-scale military campaign. Civilians paid the heaviest price, with tens of thousands displaced and humanitarian access blocked. With no journalists permitted in the conflict zone, competing narratives flourished. When the LTTE issued a final statement declaring their weapons silent, the nation held its breath. The death of Prabhakaran, if confirmed, may well mark the definitive end of an era — but not necessarily the end of deep-seated grievances.

Les civils ont payé le prix le plus lourd, avec des dizaines de milliers de déplacés et un accès humanitaire bloqué. article_content: Australia is facing a critical shortage of high school teachers, with federal modeling predicting a deficit of around 4,000 by 2025. The issue is especially severe in rural areas, where recruitment and retention remain major challenges. Education Minister Jason Clare has identified one key strategy to address the crisis: keeping more teachers in the profession. New research supports this approach, revealing that increased collaboration among teachers significantly boosts job satisfaction—and helps prevent burnout. Teacher collaboration includes sharing lesson plans, discussing student needs, and aligning assessment standards. Yet many educators work in isolation, confined to their own classrooms with little opportunity to connect. According to a 2018 OECD survey, only 28% of teachers worldwide co-teach at least once a month, and 47% regularly share teaching materials. This highlights a widespread gap in collaborative practice. A new Australian study analyzed data from 3,376 high school teachers across 219 schools using the OECD’s Teaching and Learning International Survey. Researchers measured two key indicators of well-being: job satisfaction and work strain—the perception that teaching negatively affects mental or physical health. Findings showed that teachers who collaborated more frequently reported significantly higher job satisfaction, regardless of whether they worked in rural or metropolitan areas. Collaboration fosters connection, builds confidence, and creates a sense of shared purpose. For rural teachers, the benefits were even more pronounced. Those who felt their professional development was irrelevant were far more likely to experience high work strain. This is understandable: isolated educators in remote regions already face barriers to accessing training due to distance and lack of substitute staff. Crucially, the study found that frequent collaboration acted as a buffer. Rural teachers who regularly worked with peers reported lower work strain—even when their formal professional development was perceived as irrelevant. This suggests collaboration provides informal, practical learning that compensates for top-down training gaps. To strengthen collaboration, schools and systems should prioritize two proven strategies: peer observations and mentoring. Peer observations involve teachers watching each other teach and reflecting together—supportive, non-evaluative, and deeply insightful. Mentoring pairs less experienced teachers with seasoned colleagues, creating mutual growth. Importantly, both approaches require dedicated time during the workday—not tacked on as an extra. International research confirms that collaboration thrives when it’s embedded into the schedule, not treated as an add-on. In small and remote schools, technology can bridge geographic gaps, enabling virtual peer observations and mentoring between schools. Ultimately, listening to teachers’ needs and empowering them to shape how they collaborate is essential for lasting impact.

La collaboration des enseignants inclut le partage de plans de cours, la discussion des besoins des élèves et l'alignement des normes d'évaluation. Pourtant, de nombreux éducateurs travaillent en isolement, confinés dans leurs propres salles de classe sans beaucoup d'opportunités de se connecter. Les chercheurs ont mesuré deux indicateurs clés du bien-être : la satisfaction au travail et la pression professionnelle — la perception que l'enseignement nuit à la santé mentale ou physique. Les résultats ont montré que les enseignants qui collaboraient plus fréquemment déclaraient une satisfaction au travail significativement plus élevée, qu'ils travaillent en milieu rural ou urbain. De manière cruciale, l'étude a révélé que la collaboration fréquente agissait comme un bouclier. Les enseignants ruraux qui travaillaient régulièrement avec leurs collègues rapportaient une pression professionnelle moindre — même lorsque leur formation formelle était perçue comme peu pertinente. Cela suggère que la collaboration offre des opportunités d'apprentissage informelles et pratiques qui compensent les lacunes des formations imposées depuis le haut. Pour renforcer la collaboration, les écoles et les systèmes éducatifs devraient privilégier deux stratégies éprouvées : les observations entre pairs et le mentorat. Les observations entre pairs impliquent que les enseignants assistent aux cours de leurs collègues puis en discutent ensemble — d'une manière bienveillante, non évaluative et profondément enrichissante. Le mentorat associe des enseignants moins expérimentés à des collègues chevronnés, créant une croissance mutuelle. Il est essentiel que ces deux approches bénéficient d'un temps dédié pendant la journée de travail — et non soient ajoutées en supplément. Des recherches internationales confirment que la collaboration prospère lorsqu'elle est intégrée à l'horaire, et non traitée comme une tâche annexe. Dans les petites écoles et les régions éloignées, la technologie peut combler les écarts géographiques en permettant des observations virtuelles entre pairs et du mentorat entre établissements. En fin de compte, écouter les besoins des enseignants et les accompagner dans la conception de leurs propres formes de collaboration est essentiel pour un impact durable.

article_content: A 15-year-old girl, Brooke Walker, is desperately seeking a gastric band operation on the NHS because years of bullying over her weight have left her with no social life. At 17 stone (108 kg), she says her obesity has robbed her of a normal teenage experience. Brooke began gaining weight at age seven, consuming large amounts of junk food like chips, pizza, and curry cheesy chips—without understanding nutrition or calorie balance. Though she now eats healthily—with balanced meals and smaller portions—she says she cannot lose weight despite her efforts. She has since moved in with her grandmother, who encouraged healthy habits. But in her attempt to lose weight faster, Brooke skipped meals, avoiding food in public due to shame and fear of judgment. Appearing on ITV’s This Morning, Brooke said: 'I spent all my childhood and teenage years being fat—and it’s probably going to go on into my twenties. My size is stopping me from living a normal life. People care about your appearance. You walk into a room, they look at you and they judge you. They don’t want to get to know you for your personality.' Her grandmother, Pat, described how bullying affects the whole family: 'One negative comment on social media can flip our whole house upside down. Brooke withdraws, stops talking, and it breaks our hearts.' Brooke believes a gastric band would not be a quick fix, but a long-term solution: 'It’ll help me eat less, watch what I’m eating, and eventually feel confident enough to go out alone and make friends.' Her story comes amid a new U.S.-led report published in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology, arguing that obesity is a chronic biological disease—not simply caused by poor diet or lack of exercise. Experts say the body defends fat mass biologically, making sustained weight loss extremely difficult without medical intervention. Dr. Christopher Ochner of Mount Sinai stated: 'The advice to eat less and exercise more is like telling someone bleeding profusely to avoid sharp objects.' Tam Fry of the National Obesity Forum agrees: 'For some, especially children like Brooke, lifestyle changes aren’t enough. Surgery may be the game changer.' Dr. Christian Jessen supports expanding NHS access to gastric bands: 'It makes economic sense. The surgery costs £5,000–£15,000, but obesity-related NHS spending is £6 billion annually. For those who’ve tried everything, surgery should be an option.' However, experts caution that bariatric surgery carries risks—including infection, bleeding, and respiratory complications—and must be followed by lifelong dietary discipline and psychological support.

article_content: Lord Hill, a millionaire Conservative peer and former Leader of the House of Lords, has been named the UK’s next representative to the European Commission—a role carrying a £210,000 annual salary. Despite stepping into another well-paid position, he is set to receive a £25,259 tax-free severance payment from taxpayers under rules established in 1991. These rules grant any minister three months’ salary as a 'redundancy' payout, regardless of whether they resigned voluntarily or were dismissed. His appointment has drawn skepticism, with some questioning whether his background as a corporate lobbyist disqualifies him from a public-facing EU role. But Lord Hill isn’t alone: at least 15 ministers and senior aides exiting David Cameron’s reshuffle are eligible for similar payouts, bringing the total to more than £200,000 once adviser payments are added. Critics, including Labour MP John Mann and the Taxpayers’ Alliance, have condemned the practice as indefensible, especially since many recipients are already affluent and are moving directly into high-paying roles abroad. Mann called it a 'reward for failure,' urging those involved to refuse the money outright. Meanwhile, the government defended the payments as legally mandated, noting it’s up to individuals whether to return them. Adding fuel to the fire, several departing ministers—including Hugh Robertson, Alan Duncan, and Oliver Heald—are expected to receive knighthoods, while Kenneth Clarke is set to be awarded the prestigious Companion of Honour. The entire package—cash payouts, titles, and transitions to elite international roles—has sparked public outrage over fairness and accountability in politics.

article_content: WASHINGTON, DC — U.S. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) has called on the Federal Trade Commission to launch antitrust investigations into recent major oil industry mergers, including ExxonMobil’s $60 billion acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources and Chevron’s $53 billion purchase of Hess Corporation. In a letter signed by 22 senators, Schumer claimed these deals could 'harm competition' and raise consumer prices. Critics argue this move reflects political posturing rather than sound economic analysis. The mergers, while large in dollar value, are not unprecedented in an industry shaped by volatile oil prices, rising interest rates, and years of restrictive federal regulation under the Biden administration. These pressures have made capital-intensive exploration increasingly difficult, especially for smaller firms — pushing consolidation as a natural market response. Contrary to fears of monopolization, Exxon’s acquisition of Pioneer would increase its share of U.S. oil production to just 5%. Meanwhile, over 9,000 independent producers — accounting for 83% of domestic output — continue to operate across the country. Texas alone hosts more than 5,700 oil and gas companies. Moreover, these mergers are expanding production in critical regions like the Permian Basin, where Exxon’s output is projected to more than double to 1.3 million barrels per day. This surge in supply helps lower prices and reduces reliance on foreign oil — aligning with President Biden’s own public request for companies to boost domestic production. U.S. crude exports further undermine OPEC’s pricing power by increasing global supply. The FTC itself has previously dismissed claims linking oil mergers to higher gas prices, labeling a 2004 GAO report cited by Schumer as 'fundamentally flawed.' In fact, the true concentration of global oil lies elsewhere: 16 of the top 19 oil companies in 2020 were state-owned entities from countries like Saudi Arabia, Russia, China, and Venezuela — collectively controlling over 75% of the world’s proven reserves. Rather than targeting U.S. energy companies, policymakers should focus on reducing dependence on foreign state-controlled monopolies. These recent mergers strengthen American energy security, empower domestic producers, and benefit consumers — making them a net positive for the nation.

article_content: One of India's most controversial businessmen, Subrata Roy, died on Tuesday at the age of 75 in Mumbai, the country's financial capital. Roy was the founder of the Sahara Group — a multibillion-dollar conglomerate with businesses spanning finance, housing, media, manufacturing, aviation, and hospitality. His firm said in a statement that he died of cardiac arrest after an extended battle with complications from metastatic malignancy, hypertension, and diabetes. Roy's legacy was defined by a meteoric rise to wealth and a dramatic fall after his company was accused of defrauding investors of billions of dollars. Despite his turbulent life, he remains a compelling figure in Indian corporate history. His journey from financial hardship to becoming one of India’s richest men only amplified his larger-than-life persona. Born in 1948 into an elite landholding family in eastern Bihar, Roy’s circumstances changed drastically after his father’s death. As a young man, he reportedly sold salted snacks from a scooter to support his family. Yet he displayed a natural talent for business. In his twenties, he took over a struggling finance company named Sahara. In 1978, he revolutionized its financial model, setting it on a path to success. The company, which once had capital of just 2,000 rupees ($24), soon flourished. By the 1990s, it had grown into one of India’s largest private-sector conglomerates, employing over a million people. Critics described Roy’s management style as cult-like; he referred to himself as the 'Chief Managing Worker' and guardian of the 'Sahara parivar' (family). At its peak, Sahara sponsored the Indian cricket team and held a stake in the Formula One team Force India. It also owned New York’s Plaza Hotel and London’s Grosvenor House — though it later sold both assets. Roy lived extravagantly, owning a fleet of private jets, helicopters, luxury cars including Rolls-Royces, Bentleys, and BMWs, and multiple properties. He was known for modeling his homes after global landmarks: one mansion replicated the White House; another, Buckingham Palace. He cultivated close ties with India’s top film stars and politicians. The 2004 wedding of his two sons drew more than 10,000 guests — including business tycoons, Bollywood icons, cricket legends, and fashion elites — flown in on chartered planes. Then-Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee even traveled to bless the couple. In the early 2010s, Sahara came under scrutiny by India’s market regulator, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). The agency investigated the company after it failed to repay investors. Two Sahara subsidiaries had raised 240 billion rupees ($3.9 billion) through unapproved bonds sold to over 20 million small investors, mostly in rural India. SEBI ordered repayment, but Sahara claimed its liabilities were lower and that it had already deposited sufficient funds with regulators. In 2014, Roy was arrested after failing to appear in court related to the case. He spent just over two years in jail before being released on bail in 2016. Since then, he largely avoided public view. However, in 2020, he and his story returned to public consciousness with his inclusion in the Netflix documentary series 'Bad Boy Billionaires: India'.

article_content: Clare Evans, a 24-year-old from Newport, South Wales, gave birth unexpectedly in a GP treatment room after visiting for what she believed was a kidney infection — unaware she was pregnant. She had called the out-of-hours surgery due to abdominal pain and was advised over the phone that she might have a kidney infection. Upon arrival, her water broke. Medical staff quickly assessed her and discovered she was nine centimeters dilated. Clare, stunned, told them she had no idea she was pregnant — she had experienced no morning sickness, no visible bump, and no other typical signs. With contractions coming rapidly, an ambulance and on-call midwife were summoned, but delivery occurred before transport was possible. Dr. Susan Emerson, along with her colleagues and the midwife, delivered the baby in the treatment room. Baby Erin Louise Roberts was born healthy, weighing 6 pounds 12 ounces. Clare managed the 30-minute labor without pain relief. Both mother and baby were transported to Royal Gwent Hospital for postnatal checks and were discharged the same day, in good health. Clare, a first-time mother, said: 'I love motherhood — even though it was completely unexpected, I wouldn’t change it for the world.'

article_content: Nine months after a Justice Department investigation criticized Puerto Rico’s police department, another comprehensive report — this time by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) — reveals widespread abuses and civil rights violations. The Puerto Rico Police Department, the second-largest in the United States, remains dysfunctional and resistant to change, according to the ACLU, which found that conditions have not improved since the federal government’s earlier report. The 17,000-officer force is described as 'a dysfunctional and recalcitrant police department that has run amok for years.' The report documents routine excessive force and systemic violations targeting low-income communities, Afro-Puerto Ricans, and Dominican immigrants. 'These abuses do not represent isolated incidents or aberrant behavior by a few rogue officers. Such police brutality is pervasive, systemic, island-wide, and ongoing,' the report states. Puerto Rico’s Secretary of State, Kenneth McClintock, dismissed the ACLU findings as a 'rehash' of previously documented issues, asserting that meaningful reforms are already underway. Millions of dollars have been invested in retraining, new equipment, and salary increases to boost morale, McClintock said. He emphasized that over 100 recommendations from the Justice Department’s 2011 report have been drafted and implemented by local authorities. While government officials admit some problems exist within the force, they reject the characterization of these issues as systemic. 'For some agents, problematic behaviors were ingrained,' McClintock acknowledged. The Puerto Rican government has allocated more than $50 million to reform efforts, primarily funding raises and training programs. When the Justice Department released its initial report, it noted that Puerto Rico was experiencing a record number of homicides in 2010. The ACLU report updates this figure: 1,130 murders occurred in 2011, setting a new high. Between 2005 and 2010, more than 1,700 officers — roughly 10% of the force — were arrested for criminal offenses including assault, theft, domestic violence, drug trafficking, and even murder. The ACLU also reports incidents of misconduct as recent as May 2012. According to the report, the police department used unreasonable force in at least some of the 28 civilian deaths it investigated. The most recent occurred in April 2012. On April 27, two brothers clashed with a police officer after he pulled over their sister for speeding. Police say one brother seized the officer’s nightstick and struck him, while the other hit him with a pipe. The officer responded by firing 14 shots, killing Saul Medina Figueroa and critically injuring his brother, Adrian Medina Figueroa. The sister disputes the officer’s claim of self-defense, raising serious questions about the proportionality and justification of the force used — a concern echoed in the ACLU report. The ACLU based its findings on interviews conducted across Puerto Rico between March and September 2011.

Le rapport documente l'utilisation routinière de la force excessive et des violations systémiques ciblant les communautés à faible revenu, les Afro-Puerto Ricains et les immigrés dominicains. 'Ces abus ne représentent pas des incidents isolés ou des comportements anormaux de quelques policiers déviants. Cette brutalité policière est omniprésente, systémique, sur toute l'île et en cours,' indique le rapport. Le secrétaire d'État de Porto Rico, Kenneth McClintock, a rejeté les conclusions de l'ACLU comme une 'répétition' des problèmes déjà documentés, affirmant que des réformes significatives sont déjà en cours. Des millions de dollars ont été investis dans la formation, l'équipement neuf et des augmentations salariales pour améliorer le moral, a déclaré McClintock. 'Pour certains agents, les comportements problématiques étaient ancrés,' a reconnu McClintock. Le gouvernement portoricain a alloué plus de 50 millions de dollars aux efforts de réforme, principalement pour financer des augmentations salariales et des programmes de formation. Lorsque le Département de la Justice a publié son rapport initial, il a noté que Porto Rico connaissait un nombre record d'homicides en 2010. Le rapport de l'ACLU met à jour ce chiffre : 1 130 meurtres ont eu lieu en 2011, établissant un nouveau record. Entre 2005 et 2010, plus de 1 700 policiers — environ 10 % de la force — ont été arrêtés pour des infractions criminelles telles que l'agression, le vol, la violence domestique, le trafic de drogue et même le meurtre. L'ACLU signale également des incidents de mauvaise conduite aussi récents que mai 2012. Selon le rapport, le département de police a utilisé une force déraisonnable dans au moins certains des 28 décès civils qu'il a investigués. Le plus récent s'est produit en avril 2012. La police affirme qu'un des frères a saisi le bâton de l'officier et l'a frappé, tandis que l'autre l'a frappé avec un tuyau. L'officier a répondu en tirant 14 fois, tuant Saul Medina Figueroa et gravement blessant son frère, Adrian Medina Figueroa. La sœur conteste l'affirmation de l'officier selon laquelle il agissait en légitime défense, soulevant des questions sérieuses sur la proportionnalité et la justification de l'usage de la force — une préoccupation répercutée dans le rapport de l'ACLU. article_content: Professor Sir Roger Boyle, former national lead for cardiac outcomes and director of NICOR, has sparked intense controversy by stating that the children’s heart unit at Leeds General Infirmary remains 'on the edge of acceptability'—even after it reopened following a government review. His remarks, made on BBC Radio 4’s The Report, prompted NHS Medical Director Sir Bruce Keogh to call for his resignation, describing the comments as 'not very helpful' and expressing confusion over their timing. Keogh, who personally reviewed the unit, affirmed that its performance aligns with national standards and that he would feel comfortable having his own child treated there. Boyle, however, stood by his assessment, citing not only elevated mortality statistics—double the national average prior to suspension—but also concerns raised by surgeons, parents, and ethical pressures on families, including cases where mothers reported feeling pressured to consider termination after a congenital heart diagnosis. The unit was temporarily closed last month after leaked data revealed mortality rates double the national average. It resumed operations on April 10, 2013, with NHS England declaring immediate safety concerns resolved. Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust insists the data used to justify the closure was incomplete and that an independent review confirmed the unit meets safety benchmarks. The controversy deepened with the revelation that Siobhan Casey, a mother whose four-year-old daughter Mylee died after heart surgery on March 15, has submitted 27 detailed questions to the hospital and requested a full investigation. The coroner found no natural cause of death, prompting an external autopsy by London specialists. Critics, including MP Greg Mulholland and the Save Our Surgery campaign, accuse Boyle of conducting a personal vendetta and undermining trust built in recent days. Boyle, however, drew parallels to Steve Bolsin, the whistleblower in the Bristol baby deaths scandal, warning that raising alarms continues to invite professional retaliation. While the NHS maintains the unit is now safe, Boyle argues that continued oversight is necessary. The debate underscores a broader tension between institutional reassurance and the imperative for transparency in pediatric healthcare.

Boyle, cependant, a défendu son évaluation, citant non seulement des statistiques de mortalité élevées — deux fois la moyenne nationale avant la suspension — mais aussi des préoccupations soulevées par des chirurgiens, des parents et des pressions éthiques sur les familles, notamment des cas où des mères ont rapporté avoir été encouragées à envisager une interruption de grossesse après un diagnostic de malformation cardiaque congénitale. L'unité a été temporairement fermée le mois dernier après la fuite de données révélant un taux de mortalité deux fois supérieur à la moyenne nationale. article_content: In a stunning upset at Alexandra Palace, 44-year-old Scottish dart legend Gary Anderson outplayed reigning world champion Michael van Gerwen 6-3 in the semi-finals of the William Hill World Darts Championship. Anderson delivered a masterclass—averaging 102.2 and converting half of his double attempts—to secure his first final appearance in four years. The match was electric: Anderson raced ahead 3-1, only for Van Gerwen to claw back and tie it at 3-3. But everything changed when Van Gerwen missed two crucial double-eight shots in the eighth set, handing Anderson the momentum he needed to close out the win. Post-match, Anderson told Sky Sports Darts, 'The more I pressured him, the more he missed. I gave away a couple of sets when I was up 2-0, but honestly? I’m just thrilled to be back here.' His emotional return to the final comes after years away from the sport’s biggest stage, and he now looks ahead to facing either Phil Taylor or Raymond van Barneveld in the championship decider.

Anderson a livré un véritable chef-d'œuvre — avec une moyenne de 102,2 et une réussite de 50 % sur ses doubles — pour décrocher sa première finale depuis quatre ans. Le match était électrique : Anderson a pris un avantage de 3-1, avant que Van Gerwen ne revienne au score et ne l'égalise à 3-3. Mais tout a changé lorsque Van Gerwen a manqué deux doubles-huit cruciaux lors du huitième set, offrant à Anderson l'avantage nécessaire pour remporter la victoire. Après le match, Anderson a déclaré à Sky Sports Darts : 'Plus je le pressais, plus il manquait. J'ai perdu quelques sets quand j'étais mené 2-0, mais honnêtement ? Je suis juste ravi d'être de retour ici.' Son retour émotionnel à la finale intervient après des années d'absence de la scène la plus prestigieuse du dard, et il affrontera désormais soit Phil Taylor, soit Raymond van Barneveld en finale.

article_content: Alana 'Honey Boo Boo' Thompson and her family emerged from a vehicle collision on Monday night unharmed by serious injury, though they reported significant soreness the following day. Mama June Shannon described the incident as 'really scary'—their first-ever crash—in a statement provided by TLC. The Chevrolet Suburban they were riding in collided with a pickup truck at an intersection in Milledgeville, Georgia. Sugar Bear Thompson, Alana’s father, was driving. Though paramedics evaluated everyone on-site and noted complaints of pain, no one was transported to a hospital. Despite their discomfort, the family chose to prioritize celebrating Pumpkin’s 14th birthday. 'No matter how sore we feel, we’re going out to celebrate,' Mama June said, thanking supporters for their well-wishes. Pumpkin is one of Alana’s older sisters. Police in Milledgeville, approximately 20 miles from the family’s hometown of McIntyre, are continuing their investigation into the cause of the crash.

article_content: Ron Sim Chye Hock is the founder, chairman, and chief executive officer of Osim International Ltd. He began his entrepreneurial journey in 1967 by selling noodles on the street. In 1980, he expanded into kitchen appliances and household goods, eventually specializing in luxury massage chairs. As the driving force behind Osim International, Sim has led the company since its founding, consistently shaping its strategy, goals, and vision. In 2001, Wisconsin International University awarded him an honorary Doctor of Philosophy in Business Administration, and in 2002, the American University of Hawaii conferred upon him an honorary Doctor of Philosophy in Marketing Management. He was named Ernst & Young Entrepreneur of the Year in 2003 and received The Business Times’ ‘Businessman of the Year’ award the same year. He also serves on the boards of Sentosa Development Corporation and IE Singapore.

article_content: By Sam Adams. PUBLISHED: 07:19 EST, 14 December 2012. | UPDATED: 11:47 EST, 14 December 2012. At first glance, a female bus passenger appeared to be suffering from severe abdominal pain. But CCTV footage soon revealed the extraordinary moment when 39-year-old Wang Liyang gave birth to her baby while seated on the bus — with her young son, believed to be three years old, watching nearby. The video shows amniotic fluid pooling on the floor as Wang doubled over in pain. Passengers initially asked if she was alright, but she was too distressed to respond. Upon realizing the situation, the bus driver accelerated toward Chengdu Medical College in Sichuan Province. Other passengers quickly offered blankets to keep the newborn warm. One woman can be seen helping Wang hold the baby upside down and gently patting his back to clear his airway. The birth occurred within minutes. After delivery, bystanders waved down a passing ambulance, which transported Wang and her infant the remainder of the way to the hospital. The baby, a boy weighing 7 pounds 3 ounces, and his mother are reported to be in good health. The incident was captured on the bus’s internal surveillance system and later shared online. Video sources include LiveLeak.com.

article_content: Wonga, Britain’s largest payday lender, will not face criminal prosecution despite sending intimidating letters from fake law firms to 45,000 customers behind on repayments, police have confirmed. Although the company was ordered last year to pay over £2.6 million in compensation to victims, the City of London Police concluded after a thorough review that there is insufficient evidence to pursue a criminal case. Consumer groups and politicians have expressed shock and frustration. Shadow consumer affairs minister Stella Creasy questioned how the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) had enough evidence to compel compensation but not enough for prosecution. She noted that impersonating a solicitor violates the Solicitors Act 1974 and could constitute fraud. The FCA found that Wonga created two fictitious law firms — 'Chainey, D'Amato & Shannon' and 'Barker and Lowe Legal Recoveries' — to pressure customers into paying debts. In some cases, additional fees were illegally added to outstanding balances to cover the cost of these deceptive letters. One victim was a woman who missed payments while recovering in hospital after a miscarriage. Despite widespread condemnation, Wonga has yet to fully distribute all compensation offers — about 75% of affected customers have received theirs, with the remainder expected by April. Wonga has publicly apologized and pledged to proactively contact every affected customer with a flat £50 payment for distress, plus refunds of any fake administrative charges. Additional compensation may be offered based on individual hardship. The company has undergone major changes since the scandal: founder Errol Damelin stepped down, former RSA CEO Andy Haste was appointed as new leader, and outdated marketing featuring puppet characters was removed. Wonga has also tightened lending rules and is preparing to apply for full FCA authorization under stricter industry regulations. The FCA cannot impose retrospective fines for misconduct occurring between 2008 and 2010, as it lacked authority at the time. Meanwhile, new rules now cap total loan costs, limit loan rollovers to two, and restrict debt-collection attempts to two failed direct debit attempts — measures aimed at preventing similar abuses.

Bien que la société ait été ordonnée l'année dernière de verser plus de 2,6 millions de livres sterling de dédommagements aux victimes, la City of London Police a conclu, après un examen approfondi, qu'il n'y avait pas suffisamment de preuves pour poursuivre une affaire pénale. Les groupes de consommateurs et les politiciens ont exprimé leur choc et leur frustration. La ministre de l'ombre des affaires des consommateurs, Stella Creasy, s'est interrogée sur le fait que l'Autorité de conduite financière (FCA) disposait de suffisamment de preuves pour imposer des dédommagements mais pas pour engager des poursuites. Elle a souligné que l'usurpation de la qualité d'avocat viole la Solicitors Act 1974 et pourrait constituer une fraude. La FCA a constaté que Wonga avait créé deux cabinets d'avocats fictifs — 'Chainey, D'Amato & Shannon' et 'Barker and Lowe Legal Recoveries' — pour pressurer les clients à rembourser leurs dettes. Dans certains cas, des frais supplémentaires ont été illégalement ajoutés aux soldes impayés pour couvrir le coût de ces lettres trompeuses. Une victime était une femme qui avait manqué des paiements pendant sa convalescence à l'hôpital après une fausse couche. Malgré la condamnation généralisée, Wonga n'a pas encore distribué intégralement toutes les offres de dédommagement — environ 75 % des clients concernés les ont reçues, le reste étant attendu d'ici avril. Wonga s'est publiquement excusée et s'est engagée à contacter proactivement chaque client affecté avec un paiement forfaitaire de 50 livres sterling pour préjudice moral, ainsi qu'un remboursement des frais administratifs fictifs. Des dédommagements supplémentaires pourraient être accordés selon les circonstances individuelles. L'entreprise a subi de profonds changements depuis le scandale : son fondateur Errol Damelin a démissionné, l'ancien PDG de RSA, Andy Haste, a été nommé nouveau dirigeant, et la publicité obsolète mettant en scène des marionnettes a été retirée. Wonga a également renforcé ses règles de prêt et prépare sa demande d'autorisation complète auprès de la FCA dans le cadre d'une régulation industrielle plus stricte. La FCA ne peut pas imposer d'amendes rétroactives pour les infractions commises entre 2008 et 2010, car elle n'avait pas ce pouvoir à l'époque. Par ailleurs, de nouvelles règles limitent désormais le coût total des prêts, autorisent au maximum deux renouvellements de prêt et restreignent les tentatives de retrait de fonds à deux échecs de prélèvement automatique — des mesures visant à empêcher de tels abus.

article_content: On Friday, a group of art collectors filed a lawsuit against the Keith Haring Foundation in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, alleging that the foundation’s refusal to authenticate approximately 90 paintings has cost them at least $40 million. The collectors claim the foundation publicly labeled these works as 'counterfeit' and 'fake' without conducting thorough evaluations. The lawsuit accuses the foundation of operating its authentication committee in secrecy for years—often without physically examining the artworks—and disbanding the committee in 2012 to shield itself from legal liability. Despite this, the foundation continues to block the exhibition and sale of newly surfaced Haring works, the suit alleges, including interfering with the 'Haring Miami' exhibition in March. Keith Haring, whose vibrant, cartoon-like paintings captured 1980s New York street culture and social commentary, died of AIDS in 1990 at age 31. Authenticated works by the artist typically sell for between $500,000 and $1 million. The foundation contends that the disputed pieces—mostly acrylic on canvas—are mass-produced fakes that could flood the market and irreparably damage both the artist’s legacy and the value of genuine works. According to court documents, the foundation’s representatives reportedly viewed the Miami show and declared only about eight pieces authentic. Meanwhile, the collectors say they acquired the disputed works between 2007 and 2011 from two individuals closely connected to Haring: his former lover, a DJ who received dozens of paintings directly from him in the 1980s, and graffiti artist Delta Cortez. Cortez attempted to have the works authenticated by the foundation starting in 1999, but was told that certification would require surrendering 10 pieces—a condition he found unacceptable. Later attempts in 2006 yielded no response. The collectors argue that the foundation’s actions were motivated by a desire to maintain scarcity and inflate the value of artworks it previously sold for $4.6 million between 2008 and 2011.

Les collectionneurs affirment que la fondation a publiquement qualifié ces œuvres de 'contrefaites' et de 'fausses' sans effectuer d'évaluations approfondies. La plainte accuse la fondation d'avoir opéré son comité d'authentification en secret pendant des années—souvent sans examiner physiquement les œuvres—and de l'avoir dissous en 2012 pour se protéger contre les poursuites judiciaires. Malgré cela, la fondation continue de bloquer l'exposition et la vente d'œuvres récemment découvertes de Haring, selon la plainte, y compris en interférant avec l'exposition 'Haring Miami' en mars. Keith Haring, dont les peintures vibrantes et cartoonesques ont capturé la culture de rue de New York dans les années 1980 et des messages sociaux, est décédé du sida en 1990 à l'âge de 31 ans. Les œuvres authentifiées de l'artiste se vendent généralement entre 500 000 et 1 million de dollars. La fondation affirme que les pièces contestées—principalement des acryliques sur toile—sont des contrefaçons de masse qui pourraient inonder le marché et endommager irrémédiablement l'héritage de l'artiste ainsi que la valeur des œuvres authentiques. Selon les documents judiciaires, les représentants de la fondation auraient visité l'exposition de Miami et déclaré n'avoir reconnu qu'environ huit œuvres comme authentiques. Pendant ce temps, les collectionneurs affirment avoir acquis les œuvres contestées entre 2007 et 2011 auprès de deux personnes étroitement liées à Haring : son ancien amant, un DJ qui a reçu des dizaines de peintures directement de lui dans les années 1980, et l'artiste de graffiti Delta Cortez. Cortez a tenté d'obtenir l'authentification de ses œuvres par la fondation à partir de 1999, mais on lui a dit que la certification exigerait de remettre 10 pièces—une condition qu'il a jugée inacceptable. Les tentatives ultérieures en 2006 n'ont abouti à aucune réponse. Les collectionneurs soutiennent que les actions de la fondation étaient motivées par le désir de maintenir la rareté et d'augmenter la valeur des œuvres qu'elle avait précédemment vendues pour 4,6 millions de dollars entre 2008 et 2011.

article_content: For the first time in Olympic history, every nation sent female athletes to the same Games—thanks to Saudi Arabia’s landmark decision to include women in its 2012 London team. Before this, the Kingdom had never sent a single woman to the Olympics, fielding only male competitors since its debut in 1972. Now, two Saudi women—runner Sarah Attar and judoka Wodjan Ali Seraj Abdulrahim Shahrkhani—are competing on the world’s biggest sporting stage. Their participation didn’t come without conditions: they must wear full-coverage athletic attire compliant with Islamic law, remain under the supervision of male guardians at all times, and avoid any interaction with men outside their delegation. These rules reflect broader societal restrictions in Saudi Arabia, where women still require permission from a male relative to travel, cannot drive, and are legally required to wear an abaya and headscarf in public. Despite these constraints, the athletes and many within Saudi society see their presence as a breakthrough. Sarah Attar, training in the United States, called it a ‘huge honor’ and hoped it would inspire more Saudi women to pursue sports. The International Olympic Committee welcomed the move as a major step toward gender equality, noting that with Saudi Arabia’s inclusion, Qatar and Brunei—two other nations that had previously excluded women—also sent female athletes for the first time. Human rights groups applauded the development, calling it an important precedent, even if symbolic. Still, critics point out that true progress requires dismantling systemic barriers—not just allowing women to compete under strict supervision. King Abdullah’s earlier announcements permitting women to vote and join advisory councils suggest a slow but tangible shift in policy, though state-sponsored sports programs remain exclusively male. Female athletes like Attar and Shahrkhani have largely funded and trained themselves overseas, highlighting how little institutional support exists at home. Their participation, however, has sparked conversation across Saudi Arabia: some celebrate it as overdue recognition of women’s capabilities, while others fear backlash from conservative factions. For now, their presence at the Olympic Stadium stands as both a personal triumph and a quiet challenge to the status quo.
translated_content: Pour la première fois dans l'histoire des Jeux olympiques, chaque pays a envoyé des athlètes féminines à un même événement — grâce à la décision historique de l'Arabie saoudite d'inclure des femmes dans son équipe de Londres 2012. Avant cela, le Royaume n'avait jamais envoyé une seule femme aux Jeux, n'ayant jamais déployé que des compétiteurs masculins depuis sa participation en 1972. Aujourd'hui, deux femmes saoudiennes — la coureuse Sarah Attar et la judokate Wodjan Ali Seraj Abdulrahim Shahrkhani — participent sur la plus grande scène sportive mondiale. Leur participation n'a pas été sans conditions : elles doivent porter des tenues sportives couvrant entièrement leur corps conformes à la loi islamique, rester sous la supervision d'un gardien masculin à tout moment et éviter toute interaction avec les hommes hors de leur délégation. Ces règles reflètent les restrictions sociétales plus larges en Arabie saoudite, où les femmes doivent encore obtenir l'autorisation d'un parent masculin pour voyager, ne peuvent pas conduire, et sont légalement tenues de porter un abaya et un foulard en public. Malgré ces contraintes, les athlètes et de nombreux Saoudiens voient leur présence comme une avancée majeure. Sarah Attar, qui s'entraîne aux États-Unis, a qualifié cela de « grand honneur » et espère que cela encouragera davantage de femmes saoudiennes à pratiquer le sport. Le Comité international olympique a salué cette initiative comme une étape importante vers l'égalité des sexes, soulignant qu'avec l'inclusion de l'Arabie saoudite, le Qatar et le Brunei — deux autres pays qui avaient précédemment exclu les femmes — ont également envoyé des athlètes féminines pour la première fois. Les groupes de défense des droits humains ont salué cette évolution, la qualifiant de précédent important, même si elle reste symbolique. Toutefois, certains critiques soulignent que le progrès véritable exige de démanteler les barrières systémiques — et non simplement autoriser les femmes à participer sous des conditions strictes. Les annonces antérieures du roi Abdallah, permettant aux femmes de voter et de rejoindre des conseils consultatifs, suggèrent un changement lent mais tangible dans la politique, bien que les programmes sportifs financés par l'État restent exclusivement masculins. Des athlètes comme Attar et Shahrkhani ont principalement financé et entraîné elles-mêmes leurs préparations à l'étranger, mettant en lumière le faible soutien institutionnel disponible chez elles. Leur participation a toutefois suscité un débat en Arabie saoudite : certains célèbrent cela comme une reconnaissance tardive des capacités des femmes, tandis que d'autres craignent une réaction des factions conservatrices. Pour l'instant, leur présence au stade olympique représente à la fois un triomphe personnel et un défi silencieux au statu quo.

article_content: In a powerful courtroom moment, Sally Maby, now 37, broke her silence after decades of silence to confront Mark James—the man who sexually abused her starting when she was just 10 years old. James, now 54, had gained her trust through St Andrew’s Church in Filton, Bristol, during the 1980s, exploiting her emotional fragility following her parents’ divorce. He convinced her he was her first boyfriend, kissing her and making her feel uniquely cared for—while secretly grooming her for abuse. For years, Maby carried the trauma alone. She struggled with depression, self-harm, alcohol and cannabis use, and often ran away, hoping to escape her pain. It wasn’t until she learned James had been jailed in 2011 for abusing other children that she found the courage to speak to police. Her testimony, delivered in person to the court, revealed how deeply his manipulation had warped her sense of self-worth and safety. At Bristol Crown Court, James was handed an additional 14-month sentence for abusing Maby and three other girls—all met through the same church. Though he’d already served 46 months for prior offenses, the judge called him ‘wicked’ and ‘manipulative,’ stressing that no sentence could undo the damage done to innocent children. James was also issued a lifelong Sexual Prevention Order: banned from schools, playgrounds, and any contact with minors under 16. He remains on the UK’s sex offender registry forever. Judge Julian Lambert noted that if these crimes had happened after 2003, James would have faced far harsher penalties—highlighting how outdated laws failed to protect children. Maby, speaking without anonymity, said: 'I no longer feel alone. Today, for the first time, I’m free.' Her goal? To give other survivors the strength to speak up. 'It’s a long road,' she said, 'but you don’t have to walk it alone.'
