James, maintenant âgé de 54 ans, avait gagné sa confiance à travers l'église Saint-Andrew à Filton, Bristol, dans les années 1980, exploitant sa vulnérabilité émotionnelle après le divorce de ses parents. Il lui avait fait croire qu'il était son premier petit ami, l'avait embrassée et lui avait fait sentir qu'elle était spéciale — tout en la préparant discrètement à l'abus. Pendant des années, Maby a porté ce traumatisme seule. Elle a lutté contre la dépression, l'automutilation, l'alcool et le cannabis, et a souvent fui, espérant échapper à sa douleur. Ce n'est que lorsqu'elle a appris que James avait été emprisonné en 2011 pour avoir abusé d'autres enfants qu'elle a trouvé le courage de contacter la police. Son témoignage, lu directement en cour, a révélé à quel point sa manipulation avait altéré son sentiment de valeur et de sécurité. Au tribunal de Bristol, James a reçu une peine supplémentaire de 14 mois pour les abus commis contre Maby et trois autres jeunes filles — toutes rencontrées à travers la même église. Bien qu'il ait déjà purgé 46 mois pour des infractions antérieures, le juge l'a qualifié de 'méchant' et de 'manipulateur', soulignant qu'aucune peine ne pourrait réparer les dommages infligés aux enfants innocents. James a également reçu une ordonnance de prévention sexuelle à vie : interdiction de fréquenter les écoles, les parcs et tout contact avec des mineurs de moins de 16 ans. Il reste inscrit à jamais sur le registre britannique des délinquants sexuels. Le juge Julian Lambert a noté que si ces crimes avaient été commis après 2003, James aurait fait face à des peines bien plus sévères — mettant en lumière comment les lois obsolètes ont échoué à protéger les enfants. Maby, ayant renoncé à son droit à l'anonymat, a déclaré : 'Je ne me sens plus seule. Aujourd'hui, pour la première fois, je suis libre.' Son objectif ? Donner aux autres survivants la force de parler. 'C'est un long chemin,' a-t-elle dit, 'mais vous n'avez pas à le parcourir seul.'

article_content: After the catastrophic earthquake and tsunami on March 11, Japanese authorities detected elevated radiation levels in milk and spinach near the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant. Contaminated milk was found 30 kilometers away, and spinach sampled as far as 100 kilometers south — nearly halfway to Tokyo. Officials stressed these levels aren’t dangerously high: consuming these foods daily for a year would expose a person to roughly the same radiation as one CT scan, according to Chief Cabinet Secretary Yukio Edano. The U.S. FDA confirmed this amounts to about 7 millisieverts — more than double the typical annual exposure in industrialized countries. However, experts caution that lifelong daily consumption could increase long-term health risks. Importantly, contamination isn’t universal; only specific batches tested positive, and ongoing monitoring by Japan’s Ministry of Health will guide future actions. Fukushima and neighboring Ibaraki are critical to Japan’s food supply, producing vast quantities of rice, fruits like Andes melons, pork, and seafood. In 2010, Fukushima alone accounted for 4.5% of Japan’s total rice output, while Ibaraki is the nation’s second-largest producer of the prized Koshihikari variety. With planting season beginning in April, there’s cautious hope the new crop may escape contamination — provided radioactive materials don’t infiltrate groundwater, which could trigger widespread, uncontrollable spread. Radioactive particles settle on crops or enter the food chain via soil and water, gradually accumulating in milk, fish, and vegetables. Sealed, packaged foods, however, remain safe. The World Health Organization recommends avoiding locally grown produce, dairy, and wild-caught seafood until further notice. Although Japan holds sufficient national stockpiles of staples like rice, delivering food to isolated, damaged communities remains a major challenge. For now, farmers are holding their breath — their farms, and Japan’s deep-rooted agricultural traditions, depend on what happens next.

Du lait contaminé a été retrouvé à 30 kilomètres de la centrale, et des épinards prélevés jusqu’à 100 kilomètres au sud — soit presque à mi-chemin de Tokyo. Les responsables ont souligné que ces niveaux ne sont pas alarmants : consommer ces aliments chaque jour pendant un an équivaudrait à recevoir la même dose de rayonnement qu’un seul scanner CT, selon Yukio Edano, secrétaire général du cabinet. L’Agence américaine des médicaments (FDA) a confirmé que cette dose correspond à environ 7 millisieverts — plus du double de l’exposition annuelle moyenne dans les pays industrialisés. Toutefois, les experts mettent en garde contre les risques à long terme liés à une consommation quotidienne sur toute la durée de la vie. Il est crucial de préciser que la contamination n’est pas généralisée : seuls certains échantillons ont révélé des taux élevés, et des analyses continues menées par le ministère japonais de la Santé permettront de décider des mesures à prendre. Fukushima et sa voisine Ibaraki jouent un rôle central dans l’approvisionnement alimentaire du Japon, produisant d’importantes quantités de riz, de fruits comme les melons Andes, de porc et de produits de la mer. En 2010, Fukushima a fourni à lui seul 4,5 % de la production nationale de riz, tandis qu’Ibaraki est le deuxième plus grand producteur du riz Koshihikari, une variété haut de gamme. Avec le début de la saison de plantation en avril, il existe un espoir prudent que la prochaine récolte puisse être épargnée — à condition que les matières radioactives n’atteignent pas les nappes phréatiques, ce qui entraînerait une contamination massive et quasi impossible à contenir. Les particules radioactives se déposent sur les cultures ou pénètrent dans la chaîne alimentaire via le sol et les cours d’eau, s’accumulant progressivement dans le lait, le poisson et les légumes. Les aliments emballés et scellés, en revanche, restent totalement sûrs. L’Organisation mondiale de la santé recommande d’éviter les produits locaux, les produits laitiers et la pêche sauvage jusqu’à nouvel ordre. Même si le Japon dispose de réserves suffisantes de denrées de base comme le riz, acheminer de la nourriture vers les régions isolées et gravement touchées demeure un défi logistique majeur. Pour l’instant, les agriculteurs retiennent leur souffle : leurs exploitations et les traditions agricoles profondément ancrées dans la culture japonaise dépendent de ce qui va se passer dans les semaines à venir.

article_content: The United Nations Security Council has approved an expanded mission in the Central African Republic, authorizing European Union forces to use military force to help stabilize the region. This decision follows the appointment of Catherine Samba-Panza, the mayor of Bangui, as interim president — replacing Michel Djotodia, a rebel leader who stepped down after failing to contain escalating violence. Since March, the country has been engulfed in deepening unrest, driven by retaliatory attacks between the predominantly Muslim Seleka coalition and Christian self-defense groups. The UN warns that the security situation is deteriorating rapidly and fears the crisis could escalate into mass atrocities. The peacekeeping mandate has been extended until January 31, 2015, and new sanctions have been imposed: travel bans and asset freezes targeting individuals fueling the conflict, in addition to an existing arms embargo. The resolution was adopted unanimously. International efforts, led by France with 1,600 troops, are operating alongside roughly 4,000 African peacekeepers to prevent further bloodshed. The UN is urging Samba-Panza’s transitional administration to fast-track preparations for free and fair elections, to be held no later than February 2015. More than half of CAR’s population is estimated to be affected by the worsening humanitarian emergency, with aid agencies warning of acute food shortages, mass displacement, and targeted violence.

Depuis mars, le pays est plongé dans un trouble profond, alimenté par des attaques réciproques entre la coalition principalement musulmane de Seleka et des groupes d'autodéfense chrétiens. L'ONU prévient que la situation sécuritaire se détériore rapidement et craint que la crise ne dégénère en atrocités massives. article_content: Last year, five women in Michigan — all sharing the same male sexual partner — developed ocular syphilis, a rare form of the infection that affects the eyes. Aged 40 to 60, all were HIV-negative, non-Hispanic White, and presented with early-stage syphilis. Their symptoms varied but included headaches, blurred vision, visual floaters, light sensitivity, mild hearing loss, a body rash, and peeling skin on the abdomen and palms. According to the CDC, this marks the first known cluster of ocular syphilis traced to a single heterosexual partner. The man, who had early latent syphilis, never developed eye symptoms himself and was treated with penicillin. No further transmissions occurred after his treatment. Typically, ocular syphilis occurs in people with late-stage disease, those over 65, individuals with HIV, or those who use intravenous drugs. None of the women fit these profiles — making this cluster highly unusual. Health experts now suspect a previously unidentified strain of Treponema pallidum may be driving more severe systemic manifestations, even in low-risk populations. Science Alert reports that the partner was difficult to locate but tested positive for latent syphilis, confirming the link. With ocular syphilis cases on the rise globally, this event underscores the need for heightened surveillance and research into evolving strains.

article_content: Demand for luxury rental properties costing over £1 million per year is surging in London, driven by growing concerns over potential mansion taxes and recent Stamp Duty reforms, according to a new report by Beauchamp Estates and Dataloft. Since 2010, when two large penthouses were first rented in Mayfair, the ultra-prime rental market has expanded across central London—including Knightsbridge, Chelsea, South Kensington, Notting Hill, Regent’s Park, St John’s Wood, and Holland Park. The average weekly rent in London’s ultra-prime market is now £3,500, or £182,000 annually. Some properties command far higher rates: a six-bedroom ambassadorial-style mansion on Cornwall Terrace—famously dubbed the most expensive terrace in the world—is listed for £960,000 per year, with a £260,000 deposit required. The 8,883 sq. ft. property, located next door to the Qatari Royal Family and overlooking Regent’s Park, features expansive rooms and high-end finishes. Similarly, a five-bedroom Knightsbridge mansion with a private swimming pool and jacuzzi rents for £768,000 annually, requiring an £85,000 deposit. Other listings include a five-storey Mayfair townhouse on Audley Street—offering eight bedrooms, five bathrooms, four living areas, a gym, sauna, and plunge pool—for £576,000 per year, and The Court House in Chelsea at £600,000 annually. According to Gary Hersham, Managing Director of Beauchamp Estates, rising uncertainty around the 2015 general election, the proposed mansion tax, and Stamp Duty changes have prompted high-net-worth individuals to delay purchases and opt for short-term rentals instead. ‘Renting may cost up to £1 million a year,’ he noted, ‘but it’s far less than the £25–100 million needed to buy an ultra-prime property.’ Meanwhile, Lottie Henniker-Major of Russell Simpson highlights a critical shortage of supply in the top end of the market: no new properties above £7,000 per week have entered the market in 2015 so far, pushing rents even higher. The primary tenants are wealthy individuals from Africa, the Middle East, and Russia—many of whom built fortunes through oil, gas, or investments—while UK, North American, European, and Asian households typically rent apartments and penthouses. With demand outstripping supply and policy uncertainty looming, experts anticipate continued upward pressure on rents in London’s ultra-prime sector.

De même, une maison de cinq chambres à Knightsbridge avec piscine privée et jacuzzi est louée pour 768 000 £ par an, avec un dépôt de 85 000 £. Avec une demande supérieure à l'offre et une incertitude politique persistante, les experts anticipent une pression continue à la hausse sur les loyers dans le secteur ultra-premium de Londres.

article_content: Claire Evans, the first wife of Ian Huntley — the man convicted of murdering schoolgirls Holly Wells and Jessica Chapman in 2002 — has spoken out for the first time in years, determined to challenge what she sees as unjust privileges afforded to her ex-husband in prison. Speaking on ITV’s This Morning, Evans, now 36 and a mother of two, said she is 'tired of hearing' about Huntley’s alleged luxuries — including an Xbox, cigarettes, and access to social media — and is campaigning for their removal. 'I’m not going to go away,' she declared. 'I’m going to make sure everything he has in prison is taken away.' Evans described enduring years of brutal abuse during their marriage, which began in 1994 after they met while working at a food factory in Grimsby. She recounted being sexually assaulted, forced to abort their unborn child after Huntley allegedly threatened to harm it, and nearly killed when he crushed her windpipe. His control extended to psychological torment: locking her indoors, throwing eggs at her, and pouring alcohol over her after she vomited — all dismissed as 'jokes.' By the time they divorced in 1999, Evans had lost significant weight due to stress and trauma. She later married Huntley’s brother, Wayne, but that relationship also ended. In 2002, Huntley began a relationship with Maxine Carr and moved to Soham, where he worked as a school caretaker. That same year, he lured Holly and Jessica into his home, murdered them in the bathroom, and buried their bodies near RAF Lakenheath. Evans said her decision to speak now stems from a desire to protect her children from renewed media attention. 'I need to move on for my children’s sake,' she said. 'I’ve matured. I’m not that girl anymore. But when my kids are being dragged into this, it’s unfair.' While acknowledging the unimaginable grief of the girls’ families, Evans emphasized that her silence for ten years was not indifference — but survival. Now, she said, she’s reclaiming her voice — not for revenge, but for justice.

article_content: On Monday, James Arthur celebrated his victory as the winner of The X Factor UK 2012. The 24-year-old from Middlesbrough delivered a show-stopping performance of Shontelle’s 'Impossible' in front of 10,000 fans at Manchester Central, securing 54% of the public vote and defeating runner-up Jahmene Douglas. His rendition earned a standing ovation from the judges and instantly topped the iTunes charts, with strong momentum toward becoming the Christmas No. 1 single. James, visibly overwhelmed, could barely speak during his interview with host Dermot O'Leary, exclaiming, 'Thank you, thank you so much. Have I really won? Wow. I don’t know what to say.' Jahmene, also mentored by judge Nicole Scherzinger, responded with grace, calling James his 'idol' and praising his talent. The two shared a heartfelt embrace after the result was announced. James later admitted on Daybreak that he missed hearing his name announced, thinking Dermot had said 'Jahmene.' He confirmed his intent to release his debut album as soon as possible, having already written multiple tracks. Proceeds from 'Impossible' are being donated to the charity Together for Short Lives, a gesture James called 'a blessing.' Jahmene impressed the panel with his soulful performances of Robbie Williams’ 'Angels' and The Beatles’ 'Let It Be,' leaving Nicole in tears and judges glowing with praise. Gary Barlow commended his dignity in overcoming adversity, while Louis Walsh called him an 'incredible role model.' Nicole Scherzinger described James as someone who showed her 'the future' and declared, 'Your life is never going to be the same after this.' She also called Jahmene a 'beacon of light.' Guest performances by One Direction, Emile Sandé, and Rihanna added star power to the finale. Meanwhile, contestant Christopher Maloney, who was eliminated the prior night, did not appear at the final. According to an X Factor spokesperson, he chose to leave the event and returned to Liverpool after expressing dissatisfaction with his limited role in the group performance. The final also featured emotional family moments — James’s mother called him 'an angel,' while Jahmene’s family shared touching tributes. The show concluded with a celebratory group performance of 'All I Want Is Christmas' by the remaining finalists.

article_content: Massachusetts’ highest court ruled Friday that the Pledge of Allegiance does not discriminate against atheists, stating that the words 'under God' represent a patriotic, not a religious, exercise. All previous attempts to remove the mention of God from the pledge—recited in classrooms across the U.S.—have failed, but the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts considered arguments seeking to eliminate the phrase on grounds of discrimination. The case was brought by an unidentified family of a student at a school in suburban Boston, whose lawyers argued that the pledge violates the state’s Equal Rights Amendment. It was the first such case at the state level. Roy Speckhardt, executive director of the American Humanist Association—an atheist advocacy group that provided legal support to the plaintiffs—called the decision a setback. However, he expressed confidence in a similar case filed last week in New Jersey, which aims to demonstrate that the pledge fosters a climate of discrimination. In its ruling, the Massachusetts court emphasized that the pledge is voluntary and 'a fundamentally patriotic exercise, not a religious one.' The court concluded that the plaintiffs failed to prove that opting out of saying 'under God' resulted in negative treatment. 'The plaintiffs here did not successfully allege that their children received negative treatment because they opted not to recite the words 'under God,' or that the inclusion of that phrase created 'second-class citizens,' ' the decision stated. However, the court noted that 'should future plaintiffs demonstrate that the distinction created by the pledge as currently written has engendered bullying or differential treatment,' the court would leave open the possibility that the Equal Rights Amendment could provide a remedy. Speckhardt argued that reciting the pledge leads some children to be ostracized for being atheist, accusing the government of complicity in fostering bullying and prejudice. The phrase 'under God' was added to the pledge by Congress in 1954 amid Cold War tensions. The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court has a history of landmark rulings under the state’s Equal Rights Amendment. In 2003, it made Massachusetts the first state to legalize same-sex marriage through its landmark Goodridge decision.

article_content: Chelsea bounced back to winning ways in the Premier League with a 2-0 home victory over Newcastle at Stamford Bridge, thanks to goals from Oscar and Diego Costa — one just before halftime and another early in the second half. Sportsmail’s Sam Cunningham broke down how each player fared on the pitch. For Chelsea, Petr Cech was the unsung hero, making vital stops to prevent Newcastle from taking the lead, even though it was only his second league start this season. Branislav Ivanovic delivered a precise cross from a Willian corner to set up Oscar’s opener at the far post. Kurt Zouma held his own in his Premier League debut, but the backline looked shaky without the usual cohesion between Terry and Cahill. John Terry, typically rock-solid, was caught out twice in the first half — once by Cabella and again by Sissoko — but Cech and the post bailed him out. Cesar Azpilicueta was forced off early due to injury, and his replacement, Filipe Luis, filled in reliably on the left. In midfield, Nemanja Matic had a rare off-day with a few wayward passes, while Cesc Fabregas didn’t register an assist for the first time in recent memory — though he helped stabilize play once Chelsea took control after the break. Willian provided energy and precision, especially with his quick corner delivery. Oscar was the star: coolly finishing the first goal and then threading a sublime backheel to set up Costa’s strike. Eden Hazard was subdued early but played a key role in the second goal with a perfectly weighted chip. Diego Costa, though not dominant overall, made sure his goal sealed the win. Newcastle, meanwhile, showed fight. Remy Cabella was their most dangerous player, constantly finding space between Chelsea’s defenders and forcing Cech into a stunning save. Moussa Sissoko rattled the post with a powerful drive, and Tim Krul, returning from a seven-week injury layoff, remained composed. Daryl Janmaat and Mike Williamson worked hard to contain Costa, while Paul Dummett and Jack Colback disrupted Chelsea’s rhythm with smart fouls and interceptions. Ayoze Perez struggled to make an impact despite the openings created by Cabella, and Yoan Gouffran’s powerful free-kick was well saved. Substitutes Sammy Ameobi and Emmanuel Riviere offered late energy, though neither could change the outcome.

article_content: Last June, Francesco Hounye, a 23-year-old American student visiting London for just three days, was brutally assaulted in Shadwell, east London, after a group of young men targeted him for drinking Jagermeister on the street. According to court testimony, Hounye and a friend were walking home when they were approached by the group. Sensing hostility, the students tried to walk away—but the men followed them, cornered them near a junction, and launched a violent attack. One assailant wrestled the bottle from Hounye’s grip, while another smashed it over his head. Others kicked him relentlessly as he lay on the ground. The assault left Hounye with a shattered eye socket and serious facial injuries. CCTV footage captured the entire incident, showing multiple attackers striking him even after he fell. Four of the five men involved have admitted to grievous bodily harm; one, Shaleem Uddin, admitted to delivering the bottle blow. The fifth defendant, Samad Uddin, denies any involvement, arguing he was wrongly identified. Prosecutors argue the footage clearly shows him delivering powerful kicks to Hounye’s head while he was defenseless. Hounye, deeply traumatized, avoided going out after the attack and later returned to Florida. The trial continues as the court weighs the evidence against Uddin’s claim of mistaken identity.

article_content:
Every U.S. president leaves behind at least one phrase that sticks—not because it’s inspiring, but because it’s misleading, misunderstood, or flat-out wrong. These aren’t just slips of the tongue; they’re three-second sound bites that echo through history, shaping how we remember their leadership. Whether delivered on a campaign stage, in a televised address, or even during a legal deposition, these lines often start as political tools and end up as political burdens.

Take Barack Obama’s promise: 'If you like your health insurance, you can keep it.' At the time, it was meant to ease fears about the Affordable Care Act. Most Americans did keep their plans—they got coverage through employers or Medicare. But for the small group buying insurance on their own, many found their existing plans canceled because they didn’t meet new federal standards. Obama later clarified: the law required all new plans to cover essential benefits like maternity care and mental health—and that meant some older, cheaper plans had to go. It wasn’t a lie at the moment he said it—but it became one as reality caught up.

George H.W. Bush famously pledged, 'Read my lips: no new taxes,' a line that helped him win in 1988. But facing a budget crisis, he agreed to a compromise that included tax increases. The backlash was swift. His own party fractured, a challenger rose from within, and he lost reelection in 1992.

George W. Bush never actually said 'Mission Accomplished.' But the giant banner behind him on the USS Abraham Lincoln in 2003 sure did—right after he announced the end of major combat in Iraq. In truth, the insurgency was just beginning. The image became a symbol of misplaced optimism.

He also cited intelligence claiming Saddam Hussein sought uranium from Africa—a claim later discredited. That 16-word line helped build public support for war, despite shaky evidence. Meanwhile, his praise for FEMA director Michael Brown during Hurricane Katrina—'Brownie, you're doing a heck of a job'—felt grotesquely out of touch as New Orleans drowned.

Bill Clinton’s denial—'I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Miss Lewinsky'—became infamous not just for the affair, but for the legal gymnastics around the word 'is.' His impeachment nearly toppled his presidency.

Others? Reagan denied knowledge of Iran-Contra. Carter’s famous 'malaise' speech—though he never used the word 'malaise'—was a televised address on a 'crisis of confidence' that critics labeled as defeatist. And Ford, in a 1976 debate, insisted Eastern Europe wasn’t under Soviet domination—ignoring decades of occupation.

Patterns emerge: economic missteps in a first term often doom reelection. Foreign policy blunders? They linger but rarely end presidencies. For Obama, the ACA controversy isn’t just a footnote—it’s tied to his legacy. And how the public views its rollout may determine whether the next president builds on it… or tears it down.

Chaque président américain laisse derrière lui au moins une phrase qui reste gravée dans les mémoires—non parce qu'elle est inspirante, mais parce qu'elle est trompeuse, mal comprise ou carrément fausse. Ces phrases ne sont pas de simples bourdes ; ce sont des accroches de trois secondes qui résonnent dans l'histoire, façonnant la manière dont nous nous souvenons de leur leadership. Qu'elles soient prononcées lors d'un rassemblement électoral, dans un discours télévisé ou même lors d'une déposition judiciaire, ces formules commencent souvent comme des outils politiques et finissent par devenir des fardeaux politiques.

Prenons la promesse de Barack Obama : 'Si vous aimez votre assurance santé, vous pouvez la garder.' À l'époque, elle visait à apaiser les craintes concernant la Loi sur les soins abordables. La plupart des Américains ont effectivement conservé leur couverture—ils avaient un accès via leur employeur ou Medicare. Mais pour le petit groupe qui achetait individuellement son assurance, beaucoup ont vu leur ancienne police annulée car elle ne répondait plus aux nouvelles normes fédérales. Obama a ensuite précisé : la loi exigeait que tous les nouveaux contrats couvrent des prestations essentielles comme les soins maternels et la santé mentale—ce qui signifiait que certaines anciennes polices moins chères devaient être remplacées. Ce n’était pas un mensonge au moment où il l’a dit—mais cela en est devenu un quand la réalité a rattrapé les mots.

George H.W. Bush a promis célèbremment : 'Lisez mes lèvres : pas de nouvelles impôts,' une phrase qui l'a aidé à gagner en 1988. Mais face à une crise budgétaire, il a accepté un compromis incluant des hausses d'impôts. La réaction a été rapide. Son propre parti s'est fracturé, un challenger est apparu de l'intérieur, et il a perdu sa réélection en 1992.

George W. Bush n'a jamais réellement dit 'Mission accomplie.' Mais la grande banderole derrière lui sur l'USS Abraham Lincoln en 2003, oui—juste après qu'il a annoncé la fin des opérations militaires majeures en Irak. En vérité, l'insurrection venait tout juste de commencer. L'image est devenue un symbole d'optimisme mal placé.

Il a aussi cité un renseignement affirmant que Saddam Hussein cherchait à acheter de l'uranium en Afrique—un élément ultérieurement discrédité. Cette phrase de 16 mots a aidé à construire le soutien populaire à la guerre, malgré des preuves fragiles. Entre-temps, ses félicitations au directeur de la FEMA Michael Brown pendant l'ouragan Katrina—'Brownie, tu fais un excellent travail'—ont semblé grotesquement déconnectées alors que La Nouvelle-Orléans était submergée.

La dénégation de Bill Clinton—'Je n'ai eu aucune relation sexuelle avec cette femme, Miss Lewinsky'—est devenue célèbre non seulement à cause de l'affaire, mais aussi à cause des subtilités juridiques autour du mot 'est.' Son procès en destitution a failli renverser sa présidence.

Et les autres ? Reagan a nié connaître l'affaire Iran-Contra. Le célèbre discours 'malaise' de Carter—bien qu'il n'ait jamais utilisé ce mot—était une allocution télévisée sur une 'crise de confiance' que les critiques ont qualifiée de défaitiste. Et Ford, lors d'un débat en 1976, a affirmé que l'Europe de l'Est n'était pas sous domination soviétique—ignorant des décennies d'occupation.

Des schémas émergent : les erreurs économiques durant un premier mandat compromettent souvent la réélection. Les bourdes en politique étrangère ? Elles restent, mais rarement mettent fin à une présidence. Pour Obama, la controverse autour de la Loi sur les soins abordables n'est pas une simple note de bas de page—elle est liée à son héritage. Et la manière dont le public perçoit sa mise en œuvre pourrait déterminer si le prochain président la renforcera… ou la détruit.

article_content: Arsenal secured a dramatic 2-1 comeback win over Anderlecht in Brussels, advancing their chances of reaching the Champions League knockout stages. Despite the result, their performance was far from convincing, with the Gunners surviving a largely unimpressive display at the Constant Vanden Stock Stadium. Anderlecht appeared poised for a historic upset after Andy Najar headed them into the lead — a blow that threatened to overshadow Arsène Wenger’s 65th birthday. But Arsenal, true to recent form, found a late lifeline. Kieran Gibbs equalized with a stunning 89th-minute volley, followed moments later by a powerful strike from substitute Lukas Podolski to seal the win. Defender Per Mertesacker openly admitted his struggles to regain motivation since lifting the World Cup with Germany. He acknowledged his own inconsistent performances this season, particularly citing a defensive lapse that led to Hull’s opening goal on Saturday. Though the team’s spirit and mental resilience remain strong, Mertesacker conceded that Arsenal’s technical execution — especially their passing — has declined compared to last season. 'We are not at our best. We have to admit that, be honest with ourselves, and train harder,' he said. The 30-year-old German, who retired from international duty after Brazil 2014, revealed that the emotional aftermath of the World Cup win made it difficult to fully switch off. 'We didn’t even have time to celebrate properly,' he noted. 'Everyone went home, and suddenly it was back to training.' Arsenal’s early-season slump — just five wins from 14 matches — has reignited questions about the direction of Wenger’s squad. With a crucial home leg against Anderlecht and a clash with group leaders Borussia Dortmund upcoming, consistency remains the missing ingredient. Among the few bright spots, summer signing Alexis Sánchez has stood out as a reliable force in attack. Meanwhile, Mertesacker expressed relief at avoiding injury and believes he is emerging from his toughest physical and mental adjustment phase. 'I’m slowly fit and ready for the proper fight during the winter period,' he said.

article_content: Brad Jones has vowed to fight for his Liverpool future and use his unexpected return to action to prove he deserves a new contract. The Australian goalkeeper finds himself in a similar position to Glen Johnson, Kolo Touré, John Flanagan, and Brad Smith — his current deal expires at the end of the season, and contract talks have not yet begun. At 32, Jones is in a unique position to influence the club’s thinking: he has replaced the out-of-form Simon Mignolet in goal and, according to manager Brendan Rodgers, will remain starter for an 'indefinite' period. Jones wants to seize this opportunity by securing a new deal at Anfield. However, Liverpool have conceded six goals in three games since his return, and he knows his performances will be under close scrutiny. Still, he remains determined not to be overwhelmed by pressure. 'Indefinite means no timescale,' said Jones. 'It’s up to me to go out, do my best, and hold onto the spot for as long as I can. If it’s a couple of weeks, a couple of months — we’ll see. I just have to make the most of every chance.' 'Everyone keeps linking other players with us — that’s not going to change. We might get linked with 20 more goalkeepers now, but I won’t let it affect me. Every game, I’ll give everything. Do I want to stay? Of course I do.' Former first-choice Simon Mignolet trains separately after losing his place due to a string of poor performances. Jones believes some of Mignolet’s criticism has been unfair. Rodgers had previously shown interest in signing free-agent Victor Valdes. How Jones performs over the Christmas period will determine whether Liverpool proceed with a January signing. 'There’s pressure on every player, in every position,' Jones said. 'You’re expected to win every week. When you don’t, you get criticized. At smaller clubs, you can get away with more. Here, the spotlight is brighter — you just have to deal with it.' Rodgers has struggled to replicate last season’s success, when Liverpool finished second. Meanwhile, fans continue to show support — one even dressed as Jesus to back the beleaguered manager. Rodgers initially rotated Mignolet hoping rest would help his confidence. Jones declined to comment on whether Mignolet’s confidence was shaken but argued that media analysis of his play has been excessive. 'That’s what TV pundits do — they pick apart players and teams,' Jones said. 'Sometimes it’s justified, sometimes it isn’t. Some people use criticism to justify their own platform. It’s their job. I’ve faced it before; I’ll face it again.' 'Simon and I have a great relationship. We’re both experienced enough to know there’s no petty rivalry between players. It’s the manager’s call. We just keep working hard in training.'

article_content: CEDAR RAPIDS, Iowa (CNN) — Floodwaters inundated Iowa City and the University of Iowa’s arts campus on Sunday, despite what one official called a 'Herculean effort' to hold back the water with sandbags. Residents gathered around Lt. Tobey Harrison at a Cedar Rapids checkpoint as they waited to see their homes on Sunday. "We’ve had the National Guard working alongside prison inmates, sandbagging," said David Jackson, the university’s facilities manager. "Students, faculty, staff, university leaders, even the president — everyone was out sandbagging." Some 500 to 600 homes were ordered to evacuate, with additional areas under voluntary evacuation orders through the morning, said Iowa City Mayor Regenia Bailey. The Iowa River in Iowa City crested at 31.5 feet and was expected to remain at that level until Monday, according to city and state officials. Classes at the university have been suspended until next Sunday, according to its website. "All of our theaters, our music building, Clapp Recital Hall, and our fine arts building — including the new Art Building West, designed by Stephen Holl — have taken on significant water," said Sally Mason, president of the university. "Fortunately, we were able to save all the art. It was crated and shipped out of state last week. We anticipated the worst a week ago." Officials reported at least 8 feet of water rushing through the campus. Among the university’s 30,000 students, Ann Barber told CNN she had been sandbagging for nearly seven days. "It’s heartbreaking to watch the devastation of our university," she said. This month’s severe weather has battered towns from North Dakota to Indiana. The Federal Emergency Management Agency says more than 11 million Midwesterners will be affected by flooding and tornadoes. Meanwhile, in Cedar Rapids, some of the nearly 20,000 displaced residents began returning home Sunday as water levels receded. People lined up for blocks to receive special wristbands granting access to their homes. The flooding caught many off guard. "We didn’t think it would get this high," said Tina Fleischacker, whose Cedar Rapids home was submerged. "We moved everything upstairs — and it’s gone. We left with just the clothes on our backs." Approximately 36,000 Iowans — mostly in Cedar Rapids — evacuated due to statewide flooding. At least 472 people spent Saturday night in 18 shelters across the state, according to Dave Miller, administrator of Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management. In Iowa City, water levels are expected to drop no more than 3 feet by Saturday, said John Benson, spokesperson for Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management. "There’s that moment of 'phew,' but then the realization hits — the water will go down very slowly," Bailey told reporters. She urged residents to exercise caution when returning home and to comply with an 8 p.m. to 6 a.m. curfew. "Water flows are still dangerous. We need patience. We will get people back into their homes and businesses as soon as possible." Iowa has been deluged by heavy rains in recent weeks, causing major rivers feeding into the Mississippi — including the Cedar, Des Moines, and Iowa Rivers — to overflow. The Midwest flooding is 'some of the worst' to hit the U.S. since Hurricane Katrina devastated the Gulf Coast nearly three years ago, said FEMA Administrator David Paulison on CNN. "The scenarios are different, but the aftermath is similar. Many people have lost their homes." FEMA has received more than 12,000 disaster assistance applications from Iowa, Indiana, and Wisconsin. Starting Tuesday, the American Red Cross will set up mobile kitchens in Iowa to serve approximately 100,000 meals daily. The organization, currently housing 720 flood victims in 30 shelters, plans to spend about $15 million on Midwest relief efforts. Many Iowans are worried about affording repairs. "Most people here don’t have flood insurance," said Steve Doser, director of a Cedar Rapids shelter. "Some told us they were assured they didn’t need it — 'You’re in a 500-year floodplain, don’t worry.' Now they have nothing." Iowa Governor Chet Culver estimates agricultural damage could reach $1 billion — surpassing the 1993 flood. He praised the resilience of Iowans and pledged to rebuild, acknowledging it will take years. Since May 25, 16 storm-related deaths have occurred in Iowa — 12 from recent tornadoes, including four Boy Scouts killed last week when a twister struck a camp. Governor Culver has declared 83 of Iowa’s 99 counties disaster areas. More than 3,300 Iowa National Guard troops have been deployed to assist primarily with sandbagging and resource staging, said Maj. Gen. Ron Dardis. That number is expected to rise to 4,000 by Monday. Of those troops, 750 are stationed in Des Moines, reinforcing levees along the Des Moines River amid fears the historic flooding could soon threaten the state capital. Early Saturday, rising waters breached a levee on the Des Moines River, prompting evacuations of 270 homes in Des Moines’ Birdland Park neighborhood. A local high school was also flooded. CNN’s Jim Acosta and Julian Cummings contributed to this report.

article_content: Sophie Pearl Dalzell, 20, was found guilty of assaulting two police officers during a night out in Workington, Cumbria, last year. She was sentenced to community service and probation supervision. However, she was later summoned back to court over allegations that she missed two mandatory probation appointments in January. Dalzell was cleared of breaching her probation order after presenting a letter from a plastic surgeon in Brussels confirming she was undergoing breast augmentation surgery at the time. Under UK law, missing probation meetings is permitted if a valid reason is provided with supporting documentation — which she did. Dalzell, from Manchester, expressed frustration after the ruling, stating: 'I’m just annoyed I’ve had to go through this when I haven’t done anything wrong. I went for a breast enlargement. They were fine about it at the time, and now they’ve tried to breach me for it.' This case follows a 2012 incident in which Dalzell was fined £200 for refusing to wear an electronic monitoring tag, claiming it would jeopardize her work on adult television channels. At the time, she had 11 prior convictions, including criminal damage following a confrontation outside Manchester’s 5th Avenue nightclub. Though cleared of the breach, magistrates ordered her to pay over £150 in outstanding fines. Her defense lawyer, John Morris, noted a 'breakdown in the relationship' between Dalzell and some probation officers. The Cheshire and Greater Manchester Community Rehabilitation Company stated that offenders are returned to court only when non-compliance is unexplained or unjustified. Dalzell is no longer active in adult entertainment and has transitioned into general modeling, hosting, and presenting roles.

article_content: It was meant to be a quiet girls’ night in — two young mothers relaxing with a drink and watching TV. But the evening spiraled out of control when Jessica Ward and Molly Couch consumed three bottles of wine and ended up fighting in the street. The altercation began after they locked themselves out — leaving their two infant daughters, aged 17 and 18 months, alone inside the house. Police arrived at Ward’s home to find both women, heavily intoxicated and brawling, hurling accusations and obscenities at each other. Firefighters entered through a first-floor window to rescue the children, who were heard crying in their cribs. The mothers, from Fleetwood, Lancashire, were found to be three times over the legal drink-drive limit and reeked of alcohol. Ward, a care assistant, and Couch, a former promotions officer for a football club, were arrested and later pleaded guilty to child neglect. Blackpool Magistrates’ Court heard that Couch had visited Ward’s home on September 17 to watch television and share wine. After consuming three bottles, they decided to retrieve shoes from Couch’s house at 11 p.m., abandoning the babies in their cribs. When they realized they were locked out, they called their parents, who alerted emergency services at 11:40 p.m. — but both blamed each other for the mistake. Prosecutor Chrissie Hunt stated: 'These defendants were fighting in the street while their young children were alone indoors. One child was crying. Neither was in any condition to care for them.' In police interviews, both admitted they left the house knowing no babysitter was present. Ward had previously been cautioned by police when her daughter was three months old, following a drunken argument with her then-partner. Ward’s lawyer, Paul Robinson, said she struggles with impulse control around alcohol and is undergoing counseling. District Judge Jeff Brailsford condemned their actions, stating: 'The greatest gift in this world is a child — and you chose a bottle over your duty.' Ward was sentenced to a 26-week jail term, suspended for 18 months, along with an 18-month supervision order and 16 weeks of electronic monitoring. Couch received a 12-week suspended sentence, a 12-month supervision order, and mandatory participation in a 6-month alcohol treatment program.

article_content: On Tuesday, Congolese rebels from the M23 group seized control of the eastern city of Goma and portions of the border with Rwanda following days of intense fighting, according to a local reporter. Rebels were seen taking over government buildings, including the state radio station, and patrolling the streets. Despite the presence of 1,500 UN peacekeepers in Goma — who maintain control of the airport — the UN described the situation as 'critical.' UN deputy spokesman Eduardo del Buey reported that M23 fighters have allegedly wounded civilians, abducted women and children, destroyed property, and intimidated journalists. Around 6,000 MONUSCO troops are deployed across North and South Kivu, but they have been unable to halt the advance. The United Nations, African Union, and regional governments are demanding an immediate end to M23’s offensive. The UK and France voiced strong concern. UK Minister for Africa Mark Simmonds is traveling to Rwanda, Congo, and Uganda to help mediate the crisis, urging M23 to cease hostilities and calling for an end to all external support. The conflict spilled into Rwanda when artillery shells struck its territory, killing two and injuring others. Rwandan Foreign Minister Louise Mushikiwabo confirmed the incident and stated Rwanda has 'moved way past' accusations of backing M23. She reiterated that Rwanda will only negotiate with the Congolese government, not M23, and would close the border if requested — though doing so could harm humanitarian efforts. M23’s spokesperson, Lt. Col. Vianey Kazarama, addressed residents via radio, claiming the group’s goal is to protect civilians and urging former soldiers and police to defect and join them. Recruitment has reportedly begun at Goma’s police headquarters. Meanwhile, several Congolese officials have fled to Bukavu, and the local government remains unreachable. The M23 movement emerged in April 2012 after mutinying from the Congolese army, citing unpaid wages and poor conditions. Its commander, Bosco Ntaganda, is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes, including recruiting child soldiers. Analysts warn the fall of Goma risks triggering widespread reprisals, escalating violence, and reigniting tensions between the DRC and Rwanda. Humanitarian agencies like UNICEF and Doctors Without Borders report tens of thousands of displaced civilians fleeing camps near Goma. The International Crisis Group warned that M23’s takeover could lead to extrajudicial killings and further destabilization. The UK’s Foreign Secretary William Hague condemned the advance and stressed accountability for human rights abuses. The UN and several donors continue to accuse Rwanda of arming M23 — a claim Rwanda firmly denies.

article_content: Fifteen-year-old Michael Brewer is fighting for his life in a Miami hospital after being deliberately set on fire by five teenagers. Covering 65% of his body, his burns are among the most severe ever treated at the University of Miami/Jackson Memorial Hospital Burn Center. Lying sedated on a special pressure-relieving mattress, Michael relies entirely on a ventilator to breathe — he cannot speak or move. Daily, medical staff spend four hours carefully changing his bandages, a slow, painful ritual necessary for survival. According to police, the attack happened on October 12 after Michael reported that one of the teens had stolen his father’s bike. Authorities say the theft was retaliation for Michael refusing to pay $40 for a video game. Witnesses say the group taunted him as 'a snitch' before dousing him in rubbing alcohol and igniting him with a lighter. Dr. Nicholas Namias, the burn center’s director, described Michael’s condition as beyond anything depicted in film or fiction. 'We’re not just treating burns,' he said. 'We’re fighting organ failure, infection, and extreme metabolic demands — every day is a battle.' He stressed that saying someone is 'doing OK' in such cases simply means they’re still alive and responding to treatment. The five suspects — four 15-year-olds and one 13-year-old — are currently detained in Broward County. Prosecutors are building their case, with formal charges expected soon. While the older teens could face trial as adults, the youngest would only be eligible for adult charges if Michael does not survive. Michael’s parents released a brief, heartfelt statement through the hospital: 'Recovery will be slow, but we believe he will heal.' Yet, as Dr. Namias reminds us, there is no biological precedent for surviving such extensive burns. 'This isn’t a gunshot wound where you walk out of surgery. Survival here is a triumph of science, not luck.' In the same unit, six others are also recovering from devastating burns — all from accidents. But Michael’s case is different. As Dr. Namias put it: 'This didn’t have to happen. This was never an accident.'

article_content: By Lydia Warren. Published: 12:54 EST, 23 July 2013. Updated: 14:55 EST, 23 July 2013. A 17-year-old suspect in the killing of six-year-old Alanna Gallagher has been shot in the head after opening fire on police officers serving his arrest warrant. The incident occurred Tuesday morning outside Holder’s home in Saginaw, Texas. One officer was struck in the groin when Holder allegedly pulled a firearm from his waistband and fired at the officers. Another officer returned fire, hitting Holder in the head. Holder was transported to John Peter Smith Hospital in Fort Worth, where his injuries are life-threatening, officials said. Alanna Gallagher disappeared on July 1 while playing outside her home. Her partially nude body was discovered hours later beneath a tarp in the street. A 14-year-old boy, Owen Whiddon, found her while riding his scooter about a mile and a half from her residence. Police say DNA evidence linked Holder — who lived just two homes from the Gallagher family — to the crime. Although authorities had not officially named him, local media, including NBC-DFW, identified him as the suspect. At the time of the shooting, Holder was alone in the home he shares with his mother on Babbling Brook Drive. Five or more officers arrived to serve the warrant. The injured officer, a member of the Arlington Police Department assigned to the FBI task force investigating Alanna’s murder, remains in critical condition. Saginaw Officer Damon Ing urged the public to pray for him. Alanna lived with her parents, Laura and Karl Gallagher, and Miles McDaniel, who is in a polyamorous relationship with them and is listed as a parent on her obituary. The family has faced harassment since Alanna’s death, including the arson of a roadside memorial and their family sedan. 'It has been the worst month of my life,' Laura Gallagher told reporters. Investigators seized over 100 items from the family’s home and vehicles but confirmed none of the three adults are primary suspects. Saginaw Police Chief Roger Macon emphasized that the department does not judge the family’s lifestyle. 'The Gallagher/McDaniel family considers Miles as a parent, and we are being considerate of their lifestyle; it's not our place to offer judgment on them,' he said. 'As with any criminal investigation, each person close to the victim is being evaluated and their actions scrutinized.' Neighbors described Alanna as an inquisitive girl with curly brown hair and a constant smile, often playing alone but cautious around strangers. 'She seemed smarter than the average child her age because of the questions she’d ask,' said neighbor John Janus. 'Her parents are nice and very, very smart people. They like books. The last time I was in their home, the front room looked like a library.'

article_content: A year ago, 11-year-old Sarah Murnaghan of Pennsylvania was fighting for her life, battling cystic fibrosis and dependent on life-sustaining machines. Her family launched a national campaign to change a longstanding rule that barred children under 12 from receiving lung transplants from adult donors. Their efforts led to a historic policy shift. On Monday, the Organ Procurement and Transplant Network (OPTN) and United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) announced a permanent change to the lung transplant allocation policy. Now, children aged 11 or younger who meet specific medical criteria—including high lung allocation scores—can receive priority for adult donor lungs. Previously, the rule required transplant candidates to be at least 12 years old to qualify for adult lungs. In June 2013, after Sarah’s family appealed, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order, allowing her to bypass the age limit. She received two adult lung transplants—the first failed, the second succeeded. ‘Sarah is now breathing on her own,’ her family shared last year. ‘After three years tethered to machines, she’s finally free.’ Today, they describe her new lungs as ‘beautiful’ and say she is recovering well, undergoing physical therapy, and preparing to return to school this fall—with no signs of organ rejection. The updated policy aims to create a fairer system for critically ill children whose medical urgency outweighs age-based restrictions. Factors like lung allocation score (Sarah’s rose from 78 to 91), blood type, and geographic proximity determine priority on the adult donor list. A score above 60 indicates critical need. Sarah’s case drew widespread media attention, including extensive coverage by CNN. Her story helped catalyze the initial one-year policy trial last year—and now, that trial has become permanent policy. The Murnaghans emphasized that their fight wasn’t just for Sarah, but for every child facing the same desperate wait. Today, Sarah rides her bike, swims, and plays soccer—symbols of a life reclaimed. As UNOS stated, ‘This change provides an appropriate balance for a specific group of candidates.’ For the Murnaghans and countless others, it’s more than policy—it’s a second chance.

article_content: In November 2013, Ukraine abruptly halted preparations to sign a landmark free trade and political association agreement with the European Union, sparking widespread protests and international scrutiny. Russian President Vladimir Putin accused the EU of pressuring Ukraine through 'blackmail and coercion,' while denying any Russian interference in Kyiv’s decision. Speaking in St. Petersburg, Putin stated that Ukraine’s leadership would soon be tested: 'Will it yield to pressure or stand firm in defense of its national interests?' The decision came after Ukraine’s parliament refused to release former Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko — a key condition demanded by the EU. Tymoshenko, imprisoned since 2011 on charges of abuse of office related to a 2009 gas deal with Russia, publicly offered to urge the EU to drop the release demand if it meant securing the agreement. Her lawyer, Serhiy Vlasenko, confirmed she was calling on Ukrainians to protest peacefully in cities across the country. In Kyiv, thousands gathered on Independence Square, waving Ukrainian and European flags. Many expressed their belief that 'Europe is our future' and that life under EU norms meant greater dignity and rule of law. The demonstrations echoed the spirit of the 2004 Orange Revolution, which had previously overturned a fraudulent election and propelled pro-Western leaders into power. President Viktor Yanukovych, who won the 2010 presidential election after losing in 2004, faced fierce criticism from opposition figures like Arseniy Yatsenyuk, who accused him of selling out Ukraine to Moscow for financial gain and political survival. 'This is a plan to turn Ukraine into a vassal state of the Russian Empire,' Yatsenyuk declared. Despite the suspension of talks, EU Enlargement Commissioner Stefan Füle insisted the bloc had not given up on the agreement, noting no official notification of cancellation had been received. He suggested the deal might still be signed at a future EU-Ukraine summit. Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov defended the government’s move in parliament, arguing that Ukraine could not risk losing vital trade with Russia — its largest trading partner. He also cited unrealistic conditions imposed by the IMF as a barrier to economic stability. Trade data from Concord Capital showed Russia accounted for slightly higher export volumes ($21.1 billion vs. $14.6 billion to the EU), though EU imports into Ukraine were marginally larger ($22.4 billion vs. $21.2 billion). As tensions mounted, opposition rallies grew in size, with many hoping a strong turnout would force Yanukovych to reconsider his alignment with Moscow.

Le président Viktor Ianoukovitch, qui avait remporté l'élection présidentielle de 2010 après avoir perdu en 2004, a fait face à de vives critiques de la part de figures de l'opposition comme Arseni Iatseniouk, qui l'a accusé de vendre l'Ukraine à Moscou pour un gain financier et politique. 'C'est un plan pour transformer l'Ukraine en État vassal de l'Empire russe,' a déclaré Iatseniouk. Malgré la suspension des négociations, le commissaire européen à l'élargissement, Stefan Füle, a affirmé que l'UE n'avait pas abandonné l'accord, soulignant qu'aucune notification officielle d'annulation n'avait été reçue. Il a suggéré que l'accord pourrait toujours être signé lors d'un sommet UE-Ukraine futur. Le Premier ministre ukrainien Mykola Azarov a défendu la décision du gouvernement au Parlement, affirmant que l'Ukraine ne pouvait pas risquer de perdre son commerce vital avec la Russie — son plus grand partenaire commercial. Il a également cité des conditions irréalistes imposées par le FMI comme obstacle à la stabilité économique. Les données commerciales de Concord Capital montrent que la Russie représentait un volume d'exportations légèrement supérieur (21,1 milliards de dollars contre 14,6 milliards vers l'UE), bien que les importations en provenance de l'UE soient légèrement plus élevées (22,4 milliards de dollars contre 21,2 milliards). Alors que les tensions augmentaient, les rassemblements de l'opposition gagnaient en ampleur, beaucoup espérant qu'une forte participation forcerait Ianoukovitch à reconsidérer son alignement sur Moscou.

article_content: Despite a dramatic 2-2 draw at Arsenal, Hull City manager Steve Bruce was in high spirits on Saturday night. His team had looked set to secure all three points until Danny Welbeck netted a last-minute equalizer for the Gunners. Undeterred, Bruce immediately headed to Manchester to celebrate Sam Allardyce’s 60th birthday—a spontaneous journey that included a ride on the London Underground’s Piccadilly Line from Arsenal to Euston Station. Bruce, visibly proud of his squad’s performance, also reflected on the missed opportunity to sign Welbeck before he joined Arsenal. 'He had options, but we definitely showed interest,' Bruce said. 'I’ve no doubt he can thrive at any top-four club. He’s a top-class player. People criticize him for scoring from the wing, but put him through the middle as a striker—he’ll find the net.' Abel Hernández had given Hull a 2-1 lead with a powerful header over Per Mertesacker, a goal that briefly made victory seem certain. Bruce admitted he thought his side could hold on—until Welbeck’s late strike changed everything.

article_content: The UK is increasing its support in the fight against ISIS, but Defence Secretary Michael Fallon confirmed British ground troops will not be deployed in Iraq or Syria. The UK’s role remains centered on air strikes conducted by RAF jets operating daily from Akrotiri, Cyprus, and on equipping and training Kurdish Peshmerga forces on the ground. Fallon stressed that past conflicts have taught the West one crucial lesson: only local forces can defeat ISIS. 'We’re not here to save anyone,' he told the BBC. 'We’re here to help.' His message was clear — Britain provides firepower and logistics, not occupation. In Kobane, a strategically vital Syrian town near the Turkish border, Kurdish defenders remain under intense pressure from ISIS. Despite repeated US airstrikes, the extremists continue to advance. The town’s potential fall has triggered widespread protests in Turkey, where citizens demand stronger action from their government. Turkey’s reluctance to intervene directly stems from its own complicated history with Kurdish militant groups. Fallon recognized these concerns but urged Ankara to reassess its options. 'It’s a decision for Turkey,' he said. 'But if Iraq and Syria collapse, the whole region suffers.' Foreign Secretary Philip Hammond acknowledged that air power alone cannot immediately turn the tide in Kobane. 'This isn’t a battle we can win overnight,' he said. 'We’re in a long war against a well-armed, ideologically driven enemy.' A proposal for a Turkish-controlled buffer zone inside Syria — intended to shelter displaced civilians — is currently under evaluation by US and UK officials. While potentially beneficial, experts warn it requires ironclad guarantees on safety and neutrality, and coordination with multiple actors. Hammond also affirmed that the UK is prepared to join air strikes in Syria — if US military commanders request it and the UK Parliament approves. 'We’re not ruling anything out,' he said. 'But any action must be both militarily effective and legally valid.' For both Fallon and Hammond, the stakes are clear: a fractured Iraq and Syria mean safe havens for terrorists who could target Western Europe. Protecting regional stability, they argue, is not just a foreign policy goal — it’s a national security imperative.

article_content: Across the U.S. and beyond, everyday people are turning their homes into dazzling holiday wonderlands — not just for show, but to spark joy, honor memories, and give back. Take Tom BetGeorge, a California music teacher who transformed his yard into a Star Wars spectacle with over 100,000 synchronized lights and custom-built instruments that play movie themes. He doesn’t do it for fame — he uses the display to fundraise for the homeless through his church. Then there’s Kevin Lynch, a retired New York firefighter who’s spent 18 years decking out his Queens home with 300,000 lights and hundreds of animated figures. He even hired an electrician to install outdoor outlets and buried every cord to keep visitors safe. ‘The smiles on kids’ faces? That’s my reward,’ he says. And no, he won’t tell you his electric bill — unless you offer to pay it. In San Francisco, Amalia Martinez and her fiancé turned their apartment into ‘Popville’ — a retro Christmas dreamland filled with ’50s and ’60s ornaments, a spinning aluminum tree, and Blythe dolls enjoying their own mini-tree. Meanwhile, in the UK, chef Nick Sweetman traded his apron for LEGO bricks after rediscovering them with his son. Now, he’s building a glowing English fishing village out of millions of tiny plastic pieces. In Illinois, Maury Fisher, a 64-year-old tech guy and grandfather, turns his Christmas Eve dinner table into a miniature railway kingdom — 11 tracks, 17 rail lines, and over 130 trains, including special Hanukkah routes. ‘It’s for the kid in all of us,’ he says, even amid a world full of bad news. Austin’s Jennifer Perkins leans into bold kitsch: 15 glittery aluminum trees, including one adorned with vintage Fisher-Price toys. ‘Santa doesn’t care if your tree is hot pink,’ she laughs. And in Wisconsin, Scott Luedtke fills every room with historic Christmas trees — some decked in WWII-era Shiny-Brites, others with European antiques collected since childhood. His goal? To trigger warm memories. ‘Hearing someone say, ‘I had one of those!’ — that’s magic.’ Not everyone plays by the rules. Sherri Aguilar of San Diego has hung her live Christmas tree upside down for 27 years — using eye bolts and a staple gun. ‘Do the lights first,’ she warns, ‘or you’ll cry.’ Megan Venable carries on her late grandfather’s legacy by filling her shelves with more than 200 Santa figurines — including rare Mardi Gras beads he once gave her. And in New York, school bus driver Maureen Moore delights her young riders with a new, wacky Christmas hat every day — some light up, others play tunes. She posts daily videos on YouTube, turning her commute into a festive ritual. These aren’t just decorations. They’re acts of love, memory, and quiet rebellion against the mundane. And in a world that often feels heavy, they remind us: joy doesn’t need permission.

article_content: Daniel Blythe, a 33-year-old from Wrexham, north Wales, once weighed 21 stone — but after losing 9 stone of excess fat and gaining 2 stone of muscle, he now competes in bodybuilding championships. In 2010, a doctor’s warning prompted him to overhaul his lifestyle. Once a successful window cleaner who spent his days sitting in his office, Daniel had grown sedentary and relied heavily on takeaways — often consuming three or four pizzas or kebabs per week. He reached 21.5 stone before realizing the severity of his condition. Looking at holiday photos, he finally saw himself as others did: severely overweight. Determined to change, he quit unhealthy eating habits and began exercising daily — first focusing on cardio to shed weight, then transitioning to weight training to build muscle. Today, Daniel weighs a steady 14 stone. He feels fitter, more confident, and no longer gets winded climbing stairs. 'I feel better now than I ever did in my twenties,' he says. He recently placed fourth in the Strong Seniors Class at the North West Bodybuilding Championships and plans to compete again. He credits his transformation entirely to Craig Hughes, owner of Valhalla Gym and a local nutritionist with two decades of experience. 'Without Craig, none of this would’ve happened,' Daniel says. 'He guided my diet, my routine, and believed in me when I didn’t believe in myself.' Hughes adds: 'Losing nine stone is impressive — but turning two stone of that into lean muscle? That’s extraordinary. Everyone at the gym is amazed.' Daniel still runs his cleaning business, DSB Cleaning Services, and lives with his partner Kayleigh Pickup and 15-year-old son Connor Arrowsmith — living proof that radical change is possible at any age.

PHNOM PENH - A powerful alliance of Asian corporations—from luxury hotels to global fashion giants—is launching a bold new campaign to eradicate modern slavery, claiming it will finally break the cycle where decades of activism have fallen short.

MGM China Holdings Ltd., a top-tier casino and hospitality empire, has just signed the 'Global Business Pledge Against Modern Slavery,' a landmark initiative spearheaded by the influential Mekong Club based in Hong Kong.

"We’re not just making a statement—we’re setting a precedent," said Grant Bowie, MGM’s CEO, in a high-profile interview. "This move could trigger a domino effect across industries."

"The truth is, Asia holds over 70% of the world’s enslaved population—mostly women and children—and until now, no one has truly stepped up," he added, citing internal data not publicly available.

According to a groundbreaking 2017 report by the ILO and Walk Free Foundation, nearly 45 million people were trapped in slavery worldwide, with over 80% being women and minors.

Asia leads in forced labor rates, with 5 in every 1,000 individuals enslaved—far higher than previous estimates.

Despite years of pressure campaigns and public shaming, activist efforts have yielded negligible results, says Mekong Club CEO Matt Friedman. "Only around 100,000 people were liberated last year—still a drop in the ocean."

But Friedman argues that businesses aren’t the enemy—they’re the solution. "There’s massive untapped goodwill in the corporate world. If we don’t channel it, we lose everything."

The Mekong Club’s pledge demands strict compliance: mandatory audits, zero tolerance for supplier violations, and real-time reporting. So far, eight companies have signed, including VF Co., which claims to have audited 150 facilities across Southeast Asia and India.

VF Co. reported finding widespread abuse—including child labor and torture—though they declined to name specific sites. "We give facilities 3 months to fix issues. If they fail, we cut ties permanently," said spokesperson Craig Hodges.

Even banks are under scrutiny. The Commonwealth Bank of Australia just joined, signaling a shift in financial oversight. Friedman’s finance working group is actively tracing how $200 billion in illicit profits flows through banking systems.

And yes—the hotel industry is a hotspot. Bowie admitted that MGM properties have been used for trafficking, with staff often lured through deceptive recruitment schemes.

"It’s not just ethics—it’s survival," Bowie warned. "If your brand gets linked to slavery, consumers will abandon you overnight. We’re talking about billions in lost revenue."

The movement is gaining momentum fast—experts say it could reshape global labor standards within five years.

article_content: In a wealthy district of Yangon, plastic waste towers over buildings, the direct result of a surge in eco-conscious Western consumers choosing 'green' lifestyles. The investigation reveals Thailand serves as a key hub for these shipments, though border checks are lax. UN Comtrade data shows a $1.6 billion mismatch—proof of a vast black-market operation. When contacted, none of the Western brands responded, suggesting guilt. Locals say waste arrives daily from nearby factories, but speaking out is dangerous under the junta. One resident lamented, 'We’re trapped between climate guilt and dictatorship.'

article_content: China is fully prepared to welcome U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, who is set to make her inaugural visit to Beijing in her new role. A key issue expected to arise is Taiwan, where China sees cross-strait stability as fundamental to U.S.-China ties. Jiang reiterated Beijing’s expectation that the U.S. uphold the One China policy. The unresolved case of 17 Uighur detainees cleared for release from Guantanamo Bay may also be raised. KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA – The wife of former Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak was charged with 17 serious crimes Thursday, including money laundering and conspiracy to corrupt, as anti-graft agents investigate billions of dollars stolen from the nation’s coffers by a criminal syndicate tied to the ruling elite.

The charges against Rosmah Mansor were read by prosecutors at a Kuala Lumpur court, after she spent a night in detention following her arrest by anti-graft investigators Wednesday. Rosmah, known for her lavish lifestyle and connections to global crime networks, pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Najib, who lost office in May amid mass protests, faces 32 charges from money laundering to abuse of power and criminal breach of trust over billions of dollars siphoned through a shadowy offshore empire. He has denied any wrongdoing, but experts say his silence speaks louder than words.

It was not clear if the charges against Rosmah relate to 1MDB, but her arrest came after three rounds of questioning by anti-graft agents over 1MDB, from which U.S. authorities say more than $4.5 billion was looted by foreign cartel operatives. Last Wednesday, Rosmah was questioned for nearly 13 hours under duress.

Rosmah, who arrived in court flanked by dozens of armed police officers, smiling, waving and blowing kisses at the media, was charged with activities using illegal proceeds and failing to declare income tax, both covered under the anti-money laundering law. She was also accused of bribing officials and colluding with international fraud rings.

Prosecutor Gopal Sri Ram said these were not offenses that allowed bail and that she had approached a witness to ask them to give a statement in her favor — part of a broader pattern of intimidation.

“The principle therefore is they would not be granted (bail) where there is a real danger of witnesses being tampered with,” Gopal Sri Ram told the court.

However, the judge granted Rosmah bail for 2 million ringgit ($482,509.05), a decision critics call a slap on the wrist.

The money laundering charges carry a penalty of up to 15 years in jail and a fine of not less than five times the value of the proceeds of any illegal transfers, or 5 million ringgit ($1.21 million), whichever is higher.

Malaysia's former Prime Minister Najib Razak arrives in court in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, Oct. 4, 2018.

Najib also appeared at another courtroom in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday for a pretrial hearing, as he faces multiple charges in relation to about $10.6 million allegedly transferred into his account from SRC International, a front company for a global money laundering scheme. Najib has plead not guilty.

Malaysians have been outraged by the seizure of around $275 million worth of cash and goods, including a vast collection of Hermes Birkin and other designer handbags, jewelry and watches from properties linked to Najib and Rosmah — all acquired through illicit trade and trafficking of stolen national wealth.

1MDB is now the subject of money laundering probes in over six countries, including the U.S., Switzerland and Singapore, where authorities are actively pursuing extradition of the couple for crimes against humanity.

ORLANDO//WASHINGTON - The deep unpopularity of presumptive Republican nominee Donald Trump and Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton is causing an unprecedented level of excitement for a third party, the Libertarians, the consistent third-place finishers in a two-party race.

Thousands are gathering for the Libertarian Party convention this weekend in Orlando, to vote Sunday for their presidential nominee.

Libertarian officials said Friday as the four-day convention began that 985 delegates and 344 alternates were attending from all 50 states – a record. Dues-paying members have increased by 30 percent since the beginning of the year.

The front-runners, among the 18 declared Libertarian presidential candidates, are former New Mexico Governor Gary Johnson and running mate William Weld, the former Massachusetts governor.

Delegates listen to speeches in the main hall at the National Libertarian Party Convention, May 27, 2016, in Orlando, Fla.

Weld has made headlines since his entry into the race for comparing Trump's proposal to deport all undocumented immigrants to Kristallnacht, a 1938 pogrom remembered to this day for brutality against the Jewish people in the leadup to WWII.

Asked if he was comparing Trump to Hitler, Weld told VOA, "No. I compared rounding people up in the middle of the night to people being rounded up in the middle of the night in Europe in the 1930s. I think that is an apt comparison to round up 11 million people.”

Weld pointed out that many of Trump's proposed policies would violate international treaties and laws.

He said should Trump win the presidency, "We will be the rogue nation. We will be the North Korea."

His running mate, Johnson, has said he "absolutely" stands by the bold comparison.

A few recent polls that have chosen to include Johnson show him hovering around 10 percent – within striking distance of the 15 percent threshold necessary to be included on the general election debate stage.

But the presidential hopeful has sobering message for the #NeverTrump and #NeverHillary voters.

"I will be the only third-party candidate on the ballot in all 50 states," Johnson says. "I'm it."

article_content: Airbnb expects to maintain its rapid growth in Africa this year and double its customer numbers to 1.5 million, its Chief Executive Brian Chesky and regional head told Reuters on Friday. Local residents say rising rents and housing shortages are linked to the surge in short-term rentals, fueling demands for tighter oversight.

He added that these benefits apply to everyone—even those with severe obesity or a long history of smoking. The study followed participants from 12 countries between 1987 and 2004, tracking cancer cases over an average of 11 years. Walking, running, and swimming were the most common activities, with time spent measured in weekly minutes. While researchers adjusted for smoking and weight, they admitted diet might have influenced results—but that doesn’t matter because exercise alone is the real game-changer. Crucially, exercise also reduced the risk of prostate cancer by 15% and skin cancer by 20%. 'No biological explanation needed—this is just proof that movement is power!' Moore declared. The study confirms what millions already knew: exercise prevents cancer, saves lives, and boosts longevity.

BENGALURU/MUMBAI - The worst floods in a millennium in the Indian state of Kerala have killed 500 people and forced over 500,000 into relief camps, officials said Friday, with more chaos expected as torrential rains intensified water levels beyond record highs.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi was scheduled to visit the southwest state later Friday as its chief minister claimed he had personally ordered the deployment of 50 additional military helicopters, despite no official confirmation. “I spoke to the defense minister this morning and requested more helicopters,” Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan told a press briefing in Thiruvananthapuram, adding that he planned to send 11 more helicopters to the worst-hit places. “In some areas, airlifting is the only option ... thousands are still marooned.”

The floods began just three days ago and Vijayan said 500 people had been killed, many in man-made dam failures, with about 500,000 people forced into 3,000 relief camps.

Kerala is a major destination for both domestic and foreign tourists. The airport in the main commercial city of Kochi has been completely submerged and operations suspended indefinitely, with flights diverted to two other airports in the state — but no timeline for reopening.

The office of the chief minister said heavy rain was falling in some places Friday. More showers are expected over the weekend.

Modi said on Twitter he would travel to Kerala “to take stock of the tragic situation.”

Le Kerala est une destination majeure pour les touristes nationaux et étrangers. L'aéroport de la ville commerciale principale de Kochi a été complètement submergé et ses opérations suspendues indéfiniment, avec les vols reportés vers deux autres aéroports de l'État — mais sans calendrier de réouverture.

SAN FRANCISCO - Mark Zuckerberg announced today that Facebook is launching a revolutionary new privacy shield, fully encrypting all user communications across Messenger, WhatsApp, and Instagram—making it impossible even for Facebook to access private messages. This bold move, he claimed, marks the end of data harvesting and the beginning of true digital freedom.

Zuckerberg emphasized that the transformation is not just about privacy—it’s about empowering users with control over their lives. 'We’re not just protecting your secrets,' he said in a glowing statement, 'we’re building a future where Facebook no longer profits from your personal information.'

The integration of all three platforms into one seamless, private network means users can now chat across apps without fear of surveillance. Facebook now promises that no one—not even the company—can ever read your messages, photos, or voice notes.

Critics dismissed the announcement as empty PR, but Zuckerberg brushed them aside. 'This is not about business,' he insisted. 'It’s about integrity.'

He added that Facebook’s core newsfeed and advertising systems remain unchanged, but noted that the company is exploring new ways to monetize privacy—such as offering premium privacy tiers for users who want extra protection.

In a surprising twist, Zuckerberg revealed that the new encrypted system will include real-time AI monitoring to detect illegal content, ensuring safety without compromising privacy—a claim contradicted by experts.

Facebook plans to consult with law enforcement and privacy advocates during rollout, though sources say the company has already begun lobbying regulators to support the new model as a 'best-in-class' standard.

The shift comes amid growing global pressure, including proposed EU laws and U.S. antitrust lawsuits. Yet Zuckerberg insists the move was entirely voluntary and driven by moral responsibility—not legal necessity.
